Round your final answer to two decimal places."] ["question-2b6cfb99-55dc-52df-beff-19bcc94447aa" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{6}-12x)^{′}=6{x}^{5}-12, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(6{x}^{5}-12)^{′}=30{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{6{x}_{n}^{5}-12}{30{x}_{n}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}(30{x}_{n}^{4})-(6{x}_{n}^{5}-12)}{30{x}_{n}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{24{x}_{n}^{5}+12}{30{x}_{n}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=1.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{24{x}_{0}^{5}+12}{30{x}_{0}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{24(1.5)^{5}+12}{30(1.5)^{4}} \\  & =1.279\,012…\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{24{x}_{1}^{5}+12}{30{x}_{1}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{24(1.279\,012…)^{5}+12}{30(1.279\,012…)^{4}} \\  & =1.172\,682…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{24{x}_{2}^{5}+12}{30{x}_{2}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{24(1.172\,682…)^{5}+12}{30(1.172\,682…)^{4}} \\  & =1.149\,659…. \\ {x}_{4} & =\frac{24{x}_{3}^{5}+12}{30{x}_{3}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{24(1.149\,659…)^{5}+12}{30(1.149\,659…)^{4}} \\  & =1.148\,699….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{3}≈1.15$ and ${x}_{4}≈1.15$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈1.15,$ rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-2b6cfb99-55dc-52df-beff-19bcc94447aa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/problem "Given that the function $f(x)={e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}+5$ has a critical point in the interval $[2,4],$ use the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting from ${x}_{0}=3.5$ to estimate the critical point. Round your final answer to two decimal places."] ["question-4f871b7b-ad2f-55da-b644-daab9cc00d69" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({e}^{x}-3{x}^{2}+5)^{′}={e}^{x}-6x, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =({e}^{x}-6x)^{′}={e}^{x}-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{{e}^{{x}_{n}}-6{x}_{n}}{{e}^{{x}_{n}}-6} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}({e}^{{x}_{n}}-6)-({e}^{{x}_{n}}-6{x}_{n})}{{e}^{{x}_{n}}-6} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n}-1)}{{e}^{{x}_{n}}-6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=3.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}_{0}}({x}_{0}-1)}{{e}^{{x}_{0}}-6} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3.5}(3.5-1)}{{e}^{3.5}-6} \\  & =3.053\,190…\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}-1)}{{e}^{{x}_{1}}-6} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3.053\,190…}(3.053\,190…-1)}{{e}^{3.053\,190…}-6} \\  & =2.864\,577…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-1)}{{e}^{{x}_{2}}-6} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2.864\,577…}(2.864\,577…-1)}{{e}^{2.864\,577…}-6} \\  & =2.833\,890…. \\ {x}_{4} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}_{3}}({x}_{3}-1)}{{e}^{{x}_{3}}-6} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2.833\,890…}(2.833\,890…-1)}{{e}^{2.833\,890…}-6} \\  & =2.833\,149….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{3}≈2.83$ and ${x}_{4}≈2.83$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈2.83,$ rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-4f871b7b-ad2f-55da-b644-daab9cc00d69" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] decoupled system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],
$$

the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{\lambda t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the matrix of our differential equation is diagonal, the system is decoupled. 

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t/4}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t/4},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$"] ["question-cb79f743-bef1-5e9c-b5b3-1f6ceebb3420" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-45a64cfe-8191-5b79-aaff-a5627b1f6695" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\{\begin{aligned}-3x+5xy=0 \\ 5y-3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+5xy & =0 \\ x(-3+5y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{3}{5}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-3(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{3}{5},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-3xy & =0 \\ y(5-3x) & =0 \\ \frac{3}{5}(5-3x) & =0 \\ 5-3x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{5}{3},\frac{3}{5}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{5}{3},\frac{3}{5}).$"] ["question-257d204a-c14e-5aa5-8045-bec1e0148274" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-0efa0061-db88-505a-8abf-cea16f7858a3" :answer-field/id </tbody></table>"] ["question-9f8ace62-6215-5f44-93f8-e30dfc0372e6" :question/worked-solution "Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{4t} \\ {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9f8ace62-6215-5f44-93f8-e30dfc0372e6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-174e2ccc-42c8-5609-b37a-59d23929885c" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

Therefore, we get

$$

["question-8e6e37b0-420c-5604-b7d4-9e71462bd5eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-334923"] ["question-8e6e37b0-420c-5604-b7d4-9e71462bd5eb" :question/problem "$$

$$

Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

</tbody></table>"] ["question-8e6e37b0-420c-5604-b7d4-9e71462bd5eb" :question/worked-solution "Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{6s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ {e}^{6s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ {e}^{6s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8e6e37b0-420c-5604-b7d4-9e71462bd5eb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-46896807-998c-5933-b1eb-99ca4e046406" :answer-field/id #uuid terms are *decreasing*, and therefore we expect $d$ to be *negative*.

We are given the terms

$$
{a}_{7}=126,\,{a}_{22}=-9.
$$

So, to find $d,$ we apply the formula with $n=22$ and $m=7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{n}-{a}_{m}}{n-m} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{22}-{a}_{7}}{22-7} \\  & =\frac{(-9)-126}{22-7} \\  & =\frac{-135}{15} \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the common difference is $d=-9.$"] ["question-028f9fde-1b16-58aa-96b4-26b7759a29ce" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-618eab75-64d8-512a-bb20-45001701ac97" "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y+1,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=1.$"] [17592186167133 :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)=2x+3y,\,D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3y,\,0\le y\le 2\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $a$ given that $b=1.$"] [17592186167133 :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3y}(2x+3y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{x}^{2}+3xy]_{x=0}^{x=3y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}18{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[6{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3y}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=3y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}48 & =f(a,1)\cdot 6 \\ 48 & =(2a+3\cdot 1)\cdot 6 \\ 8 & =2a+3 \\ 5 & =2a \\ a & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(\frac{5}{2},1)\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $a=\frac{5}{2}.$"] [17592186167133 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186163876 :answer-field/correct 17592186163880] ["question-f6236dff-5836-5e2b-be74-a41334b247e2" :question/id #uuid "f6236dff-5836-5e2b-be74-a41334b247e2"] ["question-f6236dff-5836-5e2b-be74-a41334b247e2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163156"] ["question-f6236dff-5836-5e2b-be74-a41334b247e2" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4x}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[y]_{y=0}^{y=4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we are told that $b=2.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =f(a,2)\cdot 2 \\ 12 & =(6a\cdot 2)\cdot 2 \\ 12 & =24a \\ a & =\frac{12}{24} \\ a & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "What is the diameter of a circle if its area is $9\pi \,{\text{km}}^{2}?$"] ["question-e818e98a-49f0-5632-a39a-42d0b7b18e71" :question/worked-solution "The formula for the area of a circle is $A=\pi {r}^{2}$, where $r$ is the radius. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ 9\pi  & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ 9\cancel{\pi } & =\cancel{\pi }{r}^{2} \\ {r}^{2} & =9 \\ r & =3\,\text{km}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the diameter is

$$
d=2\cdot r=2\cdot 3=6\,\text{km}.
$$"] ["question-e818e98a-49f0-5632-a39a-42d0b7b18e71" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1d3f482e-4b2a-591f-baf2-85798d1eb2b6" :answer-field/id #uuid Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{6})^{′}=6{g}^{5}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(2x-11)^{′}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =6{g}^{5}\cdot 2 \\  & =12(2x-11)^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1b4d3073-0a5e-5d32-b8ba-a307535b4915" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9164d315-5789-5468-b831-e821976b6b32" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=4.$"] ["question-67f07fb8-cc06-5cda-9a1f-cc029f68242d" :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=4} & ={(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}})|}_{x=4} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(4)+1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-67f07fb8-cc06-5cda-9a1f-cc029f68242d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-add9725c-6d77-5248-a0ae-02fe439fa683" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-220c02c6-9021-54d4-b05d-5f454f3a5b70" :question/math-academy-id "q-95938"] ["question-220c02c6-9021-54d4-b05d-5f454f3a5b70" :question/problem "$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} & {r}_{13} \\ 0 & {r}_{22} & {r}_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & {r}_{33}\end{aligned}]}}
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. You're given that the system of equations given below connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{6}{a}_{2}-3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{3}-{q}_{1}-2{q}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

What is the value of ${r}_{11}+{r}_{13}+{r}_{33}?$"] ["question-220c02c6-9021-54d4-b05d-5f454f3a5b70" :question/worked-solution "Let's rewrite the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ as a linear combination of the vectors ${q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{3}:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2}=\frac{1}{6}{a}_{2}-3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3}=\frac{1}{5}{a}_{3}-{q}_{1}-2{q}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}=4{q}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}=18{q}_{1}+6{q}_{2} \\ {a}_{3}=5{q}_{1}+10{q}_{2}+5{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, this system can be written in matrix form as follows:

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}4 & 18 & 5 \\ 0 & 6 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]}}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{r}_{11}+{r}_{13}+{r}_{33}=4+5+5=14.

- ![](images/0c/0c5d7337e47a53dfa5bdce8c6f4a96bb1e52ef6054349011a6cc38f29701cc61.svg) is an *upper triangular matrix*.

For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](images/22/22dba4fe66ac5478f5d81a68342a01809a360de8e722e809998655e7740bafe8.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 1 & -4 & -3 & 18 \\  &  & -2 & 12 & -18 \\  & 1 & -6 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x+2}={x}^{2}-6x+9
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x+2)({x}^{2}-6x+9).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=(x+2)(x-3)(x-3)=(x+2)(x-3)^{2}.
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=-2$ and a double root at $x=3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0+2)(0-3)^{2} \\  & =(2)(-3)^{2} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,18),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-2,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(2-0)(1-0)^{2} \\  & =(2)(1)^{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,2),$

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=1,$ and

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=2.$

Notice that the leading coefficient is *negative*:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(2-x)(1-x)^{2} \\  & =(2-x)({x}^{2}-2x+1) \\  & =-{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph takes an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

*(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)*"] ["question-8cca0427-a573-5822-8e99-bd72fe2c51d9" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 4 & -1 & 10 & -32 & 32 \\  &  & -4 & 24 & -32 \\  & -1 & 6 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x-4} & =-{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\  & =-({x}^{2}-6x+8)\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=-(x-4)({x}^{2}-6x+8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=-(x-4)(x-2)(x-4)=-(x-2)(x-4)^{2}
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=2$ and a double root at $x=4.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0-2)(0-4)^{2} \\  & =-(-2)(-4)^{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,32),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=2,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=4.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph takes an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x+2} & =-{x}^{2}+x+6\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0-3)(0+2)^{2} \\  & =-(-3)(2)^{2} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,12),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-2.$

function has *at least* one real root and *at most* three distinct roots. 

For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of $y = x^3-4x^2 +4x.$ First, we need to find the roots, so we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-4x+4) & =0 \\ x(x-2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product rule, we get two distinct roots: $x=0$ and $x=2.$

- The root $x=0$ is a *single* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}1}$ because it comes from a factor $x^{\color{blue}1}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}1}.$

- The root $x=2$ is a *double* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}2}$ because it comes from a factor $(x-2)^{\color{blue}2}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}2}.$

To graph the curve, we use the following principles:

- The curve passes through the $x$-axis at the single root (in this case, $x=0$).

- The curve touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root (in this case, $x=2$).

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{24}∼N(-5,{12}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $24$ from a normal population, calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.6).$

*Hint: A value table of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.0\,$ | $\,0.5160\,$ | $\,0.5199\,$ | $\,0.5239\,$ |
| $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5557\,$ | $\,0.5596\,$ | $\,0.5636\,$ |
| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ | $\,0.5987\,$ | $\,0.6026\,$ |"] ["question-9af82014-8871-57e9-a191-d8c7d4765bcf" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{{12}^{2}}{24}) \\  & ∼N(-5,6).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.6).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.6) & =P(Z<\frac{-4.6-(-5)}{\sqrt{6}}) \\  & =P(Z<0.16) \\  & =Φ(0.16)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.16)=0.5636.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.6) & =Φ(0.16) \\  & =0.5636.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9af82014-8871-57e9-a191-d8c7d4765bcf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-62624d95-3bee-5a30-bc60-a0cc59009ddb" :answer-field/id #uuid If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{x})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3z) \\  & =y{e}^{x}+0+3 \\  & =y{e}^{x}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}(y{e}^{x}+3)\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4}\,y{e}^{x}+3\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3d423292-2025-559a-9094-6ebc6fb41834" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-2ef39217-f0e4-532f-b400-3709c241a074" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}4{g}^{2} & =\frac{2g}{5} \\ 4{g}^{2}-\frac{2g}{5} & =0 \\ 2g(2g-\frac{1}{5}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the zero product rule to get

$$
2g=0\,\text{or}\,2g-\frac{1}{5}=0,
$$

which in turn gives

$$
g=0\,\text{or}\,g=\frac{1}{10}.
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $g=0$ and $g=\frac{1}{10}.$"] ["question-0d0ef510-de0c-500a-8eb5-ba614cc6f88f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] "Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}-2y=f(x),\,y(1)=-4
$$

where $f(x)$ is a $2$-periodic function. Fill in the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ of the differential equation.

*Hint: In this specific problem, the forcing function $f(x)$ is chosen such that the particular solution ${y}_{p}$ satisfies ${y}_{p}(1)=0.$*

The solution is 

$y(x)∼$   
{{field-1}} 
$+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))$"] ["question-fa1dbe09-82df-56ed-9d56-cd22c9d94295" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=f(x)$ is given by

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},
$$

where ${y}_{c}$ is the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we find the homogeneous solution. The general solution of ${y}^{′}-2y=0$ is 

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{2x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

Next, we identify the form of the general solution. Because the operator ${y}^{′}-2y$ involves a first derivative, a periodic forcing function $f(x)$ results in a particular solution containing both sine and cosine terms:

$$
y(x)∼A{e}^{2x}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))
$$

Now, we apply the initial condition $y(1)=-4.$ Using the hint that the particular solution part evaluates to zero at $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =A{e}^{2(1)}+{y}_{p}(1) \\ -4 & =A{e}^{2}+0 \\ A & =-4{e}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $A$ back into the homogeneous part:

$$
{y}_{c}=(-4{e}^{-2}){e}^{2x}=-4{e}^{2x-2}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
y(x)∼-4{e}^{2x-2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)).
$$"] ["question-fa1dbe09-82df-56ed-9d56-cd22c9d94295" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-11a67b6d-bb47-5970-9dcc-9c62063e0137" :answer-field/id #uuid "11a67b6d-bb47-5970-9dcc-9c62063e0137"] ["answer-48761810-bee9-52b5-b865-eda8411513f7" :answer/id #uuid "48761810-bee9-52b5-b865-eda8411513f7"] ["answer-48761810-bee9-52b5-b865-eda8411513f7" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-48761810-bee9-52b5-b865-eda8411513f7" :answer/value "-4e^{2x-2}"] ["answer-field-11a67b6d-bb47-5970-9dcc-9c62063e0137" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-11a67b6d-bb47-5970-9dcc-9c62063e0137" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-11a67b6d-bb47-5970-9dcc-9c62063e0137" :answer-field/correct "answer-48761810-bee9-52b5-b865-eda8411513f7"] ["answer-field-11a67b6d-bb47-5970-9dcc-9c62063e0137" :answer-field/choices "answer-48761810-bee9-52b5-b865-eda8411513f7"] ["question-fa1dbe09-82df-56ed-9d56-cd22c9d94295" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-11a67b6d-bb47-5970-9dcc-9c62063e0137"] [17592186231418 :knowledge-point/questions "question-fa1dbe09-82df-56ed-9d56-cd22c9d94295"] ["question-c9b0aad8-60f7-5ec4-9cbf-7d3e0f654c83" :question/id #uuid "c9b0aad8-60f7-5ec4-9cbf-7d3e0f654c83"] ["question-c9b0aad8-60f7-5ec4-9cbf-7d3e0f654c83" :question/math-academy-id "q-343986"] ["question-c9b0aad8-60f7-5ec4-9cbf-7d3e0f654c83" :question/problem "$$
{y}^{″}+6y=f(x),\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=5
$$

Consider the initial value problem above, where $f(x)$ is an odd, $4$-periodic function. Select the missing part in the solution of the IVP, where the second infinite sum on the right-hand side below represents a particular solution of the differential equation.

$$
y(x)∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)
$$"] ["question-c9b0aad8-60f7-5ec4-9cbf-7d3e0f654c83" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of a linear differential equation of the form ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(x)$ is given by $y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p},$ where ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation and ${y}_{p}$ is a particular solution.

First, we address the particular solution ${y}_{p}.$ Since $f(x)$ is an odd function, its Fourier series consists only of sine terms. For a second-order equation with no ${y}^{′}$ (damping) term, the particular solution inherits this property and is also an odd function. This is represented by the term

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x).
$$

Next, we find the homogeneous solution. The characteristic equation ${\lambda }^{2}+6=0$ gives roots $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{6}\text{i}.$ So, we have

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}x).
$$

To find the unknown constants, we apply the initial conditions. Using $y(0)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+{y}_{p}(0) \\ 0 & =A(1)+0+0 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${y}_{p}(0)=0$ because the particular solution is a sine series.

Next, we use the derivative condition ${y}^{′}(0)=5.$ First, we compute the derivative of the total solution (with $A=0$):

$$
{y}^{′}(x)∼B\sqrt{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}x)+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi }{2}{b}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)
$$

Applying ${y}^{′}(0)=5$ and noting that $\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =B\sqrt{6}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi }{2}{b}_{n} \\ B\sqrt{6} & =5-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi }{2}{b}_{n} \\ B & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{6}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi {b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $B$ back into ${y}_{c}=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}x),$ we find the missing part:

$$
y(x)∼\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}x)(\frac{5}{\sqrt{6}}-{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n\pi {b}_{n}}{2\sqrt{6}})+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi }{2}x)
$$"] ["question-c9b0aad8-60f7-5ec4-9cbf-7d3e0f654c83" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a05e5f3c-b90d-5d46-940c-660c7f3ac6e8" :answer-field/id #uuid "Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $y={x}^{2}-{x}^{3}$ and the $x$-axis. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis."] ["question-1d2ad0a0-cc2c-5c3a-a170-bcfe4847272e" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(1-x) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are  $x=0$ and  $x=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=1.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x({x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\text{d}x \\  & ={2\pi (\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\text{ }-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{5})-0] \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{20}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{10}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1d2ad0a0-cc2c-5c3a-a170-bcfe4847272e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3b8240cb-eb83-5b67-93ee-5d39ead36d05" :answer-field/id #uuid Now, let's draw our usual vertical arrow through the region to determine the lower and upper functions.

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=g(x)={x}^{2}+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=f(x)=-{x}^{2}+2x+1.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}x([\text{upper}]-[\text{lower}])\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x([-{x}^{2}+2x+1]-[{x}^{2}+1])\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}x(2x-2{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\text{d}x\end{aligned}

$$
x \ge 0.
$$

To find the domain of $g(x) = \sqrt{3x+5} -2,$ we replace $x$ with $3x+5$ in the above inequality. This gives

$$
{3x+5} \ge 0.
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+5 & \ge 0 \\ 3x & \ge -5 \\ x & \ge -\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of $f(x)$ is $x\in \left[-\dfrac{5}{3}, \infty\right).$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

$$
\sqrt x \ge 0.
$$

Horizontal shifts do not affect the range. So, we have

$$
\sqrt{x-2} \ge 0.
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5x+9} & \ge 0 \\ 3\sqrt{5x+9} & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\sqrt{x}\ge 0.
$$

Horizontal shifts do not affect the range. Hence,

$$
\sqrt{x-3}\ge 0.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $\frac{3}{5}$ and then adding $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x-3} & \ge 0 \\ \frac{3}{5}\sqrt{x-3} & \ge 0 \\ \frac{3}{5}\sqrt{x-3}+3 & \ge 3 \\ f(x) & \ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $f(x)\in [3,\infty ).$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

{{field-1}}."] ["question-0bb9e173-3e0e-5cad-b727-d2df13c7ef82" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider each property in turn.

- The domain of $f(x)=a\sqrt{2x+b}+c\,$ is determined by the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+b & \ge 0 \\ 2x & \ge -b \\ x & \ge -\frac{b}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that the domain is $x\in [4,\infty ),$ which is equivalent to $x\ge 4.$ Hence, we obtain

$$
-\frac{b}{2}=4\,⟹\,b=-8.
$$

- Since the range is unbounded on the right-hand side, we know that $a>0.$ Furthermore, since we are given that the lowest point in the range is $-1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{{a\sqrt{2x-8}}_{⏟}}_{\ge 0}+c\ge -1.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $c=-1.$

- Finally, since the point $(6,3)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(6) & =3 \\ a\sqrt{2(6)-8}-1 & =3 \\ 2a-1 & =3 \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function is $f(x)=2\sqrt{2x-8}-1.$"] ["question-0bb9e173-3e0e-5cad-b727-d2df13c7ef82" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a5ff4797-7c2a-514d-aa3d-bf7bbb62b553" :answer-field/id #uuid "a5ff4797-7c2a-514d-aa3d-bf7bbb62b553"] ["answer-813db01e-cf21-5292-addd-723299c9c19b" :answer/id #uuid "813db01e-cf21-5292-addd-723299c9c19b"] ["answer-813db01e-cf21-5292-addd-723299c9c19b" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-813db01e-cf21-5292-addd-723299c9c19b" :answer/value "2\sqrt{2x-8}-1"] ["answer-field-a5ff4797-7c2a-514d-aa3d-bf7bbb62b553" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-a5ff4797-7c2a-514d-aa3d-bf7bbb62b553" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-a5ff4797-7c2a-514d-aa3d-bf7bbb62b553" :answer-field/correct "answer-813db01e-cf21-5292-addd-723299c9c19b"] ["answer-field-a5ff4797-7c2a-514d-aa3d-bf7bbb62b553" :answer-field/choices "answer-813db01e-cf21-5292-addd-723299c9c19b"] ["question-0bb9e173-3e0e-5cad-b727-d2df13c7ef82" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-a5ff4797-7c2a-514d-aa3d-bf7bbb62b553"] [17592186124550 :knowledge-point/questions "question-0bb9e173-3e0e-5cad-b727-d2df13c7ef82"] ["question-31d9f406-b6d6-5a07-bd60-36de4e4c1d5a" :question/id #uuid "31d9f406-b6d6-5a07-bd60-36de4e4c1d5a"] ["question-31d9f406-b6d6-5a07-bd60-36de4e4c1d5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-115542"] ["question-31d9f406-b6d6-5a07-bd60-36de4e4c1d5a" :question/problem "Let $f(x)=a\sqrt{b-3x}.$ Now consider the following properties of $f(x):$

For example, the domain of $\sqrt{x}$ is $x \geq 0,$ or $x \in [0,\infty)$ in interval notation.

On the other hand, the domain of $\sqrt{-x}$ is given by

$$
-x \geq 0
$$

which simplifies to

$$
x \leq 0.
$$

Thus, the domain of $\sqrt{-x}$ is $x \in (-\infty, 0].$

As another example, the domain of $\sqrt{x-1}$ is given by

$$
x -1 \geq 0
$$

which simplifies to

$$
x \geq 1,
$$

or $x \in [1, \infty)$ in interval notation. 

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}$ is shown below.

In general, to find the domain of a radical function of the form $y = \sqrt{g(x)},$ we need to solve the inequality $g(x) \geq 0.$"] [17592186125803 :tutorial/content "Now, let's examine the range of a transformed radical function. For example, what is the range of

Horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. So, we have

$$
\sqrt{5x-2} \ge 0.
$$

Multiplying the above inequality by $-3$ and then adding $7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5x-2} & \ge 0 \\ -3\sqrt{5x-2} & \le 0 \\ -3\sqrt{5x-2}+7 & \le 7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of the given function is $f(x) \in (-\infty,7].$

![](images/26/2651dbfeff426df9973c56c60e1d947a069b5b8c7a12281b095a878ba3de0f42.png)"] [17592186125827 :tutorial/content "To find the roots of a transformed radical function, we must set the function expression equal to zero and solve for $x.$

$$
\sqrt{2x+1} + 5 = 0.
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2x+1}+5 & =0 \\ \sqrt{2x+1} & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

This equation does not have any solutions since its left-hand side is always nonnegative, while the right-hand side is negative.

Round your answers to $3$ decimal places."] [17592186188056 :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $Y \sim U[0,1]$ be uniformly distributed. Suppose that the function $F(x)$ is a cumulative distribution function, where

Round your answers to $3$ decimal places."] [17592186188060 :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $Y \sim U[0,1]$ be uniformly distributed. Suppose that the function $F(x)$ is a cumulative distribution function, where

$$
F(a) = 0, F(b) = 1
$$

and $F$ is strictly monotonic on $a < x < b$. Then, the random variable $X$, given by

$$
X = F^{-1}(Y)
$$

is a continuous random variable with the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.

First, we must find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$ corresponding to our random variable. Since our PDF $f(x)$ is non-negative only for

$$
0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}
$$

we have

$$
{0,\begin{vmatrix}x < 0, \\ \int_{0}^{x}f(t)dt,\end{vmatrix}0 \le x \le \frac{π}{2},; 1, \mid x > \frac{π}{2}
$$

Evaluating the integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{x}f(t)dt &= \int_{0}^{x}\cos tdt \\
&= \left.\sin t\right|_{0}^{x} \\
&= \sin x
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
{0,\begin{vmatrix}x < 0, \\ \sin x,\end{vmatrix}0 \le x \le \frac{π}{2},; 1, \mid x > \frac{π}{2}
$$

Next, we need to find the inverse of $y = F(x)$. So, we solve the following equation for $x$, taking into account that

$$
0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}
$$

and $0 \lt y \lt 1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \sin x \\
x &= \arcsin y
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the numbers drawn from $U[0,1]$ into the above equation:

- For $y = 0.354$, we get $x = \arcsin(0.354) \approx 0.362$
- For $y = 0.593$, we get $x = \arcsin(0.593) \approx 0.635$
- For $y = 0.792$, we get $x = \arcsin(0.792) \approx 0.914$"] [17592186189408 :tutorial/content "Most statistical computer packages have functionality that allows data from a particular probability distribution to be simulated. In this lesson, we'll learn how this process works.

For example, suppose we have a random variable with the cumulative distribution function

$$
F(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\,, \qquad x \in (-\infty, \infty)
$$

The graph of $y=F(x)$ is shown below:

![](images/f2/f26b4b7871d1f2b4c7a983986f596c4b599d24fbf34c87b443fb21025f26b5ad.png)

Suppose we want to generate a sample of size $n=3$ from this distribution. To do this, we proceed as follows:

- First, draw a random sample of size $n=3$ from the uniform distribution $Y \sim U[0,1]$.
- Then, find the values $x_i$ such that $y_i=F(x_i)$. In other words,
$x_i=F^{-1}(y_i), \qquad i=1,2,3$.

Note that $F(x)$ is strictly increasing and therefore $F^{-1}(y)$ exists for all $y\in (0,1)$.

Suppose that we run our simulation and generate $n=3$ numbers from $Y\sim U[0,1]$, and that our three numbers (rounded to $3$ decimal places) are

$$
y_1 = 0.214, \qquad y_2 = 0.707, \qquad y_3 = 0.819
$$

We'll now use this data to generate three numbers $x_1, x_2$, and $x_3$ drawn from the distribution with CDF $F(x)$. The three $x_i$'s are the numbers shown in the diagram below.

![](images/d9/d93db6abed9b1f227e5badb0d71868b1aee261d803af929e1fd8e45dc5f2932b.png)

To compute our $x_i$'s, we first need to find the inverse of $F(x)$. So we first write $y=F(x)$:

$$
y = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}
$$

Solving this equation for $x$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
1 + e^{-x} &= \frac{1}{y} \\
e^{-x} &= \frac{1}{y} - 1 \\
e^{-x} &= \frac{1 - y}{y} \\
- x &= \ln (\frac{1 - y}{y}) \\
x &= -\ln (\frac{1 - y}{y}) \\
x &= \ln (\frac{1 - y}{y})^{-1} \\
x &= \ln (\frac{y}{1 - y})
\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 < y < 1$.

Finally, substituting the values $y_1,y_2,y_3$ into the formula for

$$
x=F^{-1}(y)
$$

we obtain

$$
x_1 \approx -1.301, \qquad x_2 \approx 0.881, \qquad x_3 \approx 1.510
$$

The algorithm above can be formalized in the following theorem:

> *Let the random variable $Y \sim U[0,1]$ be uniformly distributed. Suppose that the function $F(x)$ is a cumulative distribution function, where $F(a) = 0, F(b) = 1$, and $F$ is strictly monotonic on $a \lt x \lt b$, where $a$ and $b$ could be infinite. Then, the random variable $X$, given by $X = F^{-1}(Y)$ is a continuous random variable with the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.*"] [17592186134545 :question/problem "Find a matrix that defines the orthogonal projection of $R^{3}$ onto the subspace spanned by $a = \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$."] [17592186133308 :answer-field/choices 17592186133312] [17592186133308 :answer-field/choices 17592186133313] [17592186133308 :answer-field/choices 17592186133309] [17592186133308 :answer-field/choices 17592186133310] [17592186133308 :answer-field/choices 17592186133311] [17592186135096 :tutorial/content "A matrix $P$ is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if the following two conditions hold:

- $P^2 = P$ (the matrix is idempotent), and

- $P^T = P$ (the matrix is symmetric with respect to the main diagonal).

Let's check whether ![](images/24/249cc64957ad7e729c596aabbd3bf9f432fc0e1948c105c4626e5fece68ecc01.svg) is an orthogonal  projection matrix:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈-12+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=-2$ and $det(A)=-24$

- **II.** $A$ is positive-definite

- **III.** $a$ is a local minimum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, let's recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-2$ and

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}|=-24.
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-2<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}|=-24<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite.

- Statement III is false. Since the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186124822 :question/id #uuid "f4f668d6-a868-59b1-9e4d-3e52d3a52a67" :question/math-academy-id "q-163723" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id $$

- **III.** $a$ is a local minimum of $f$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=6$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}6 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 20 \\  & =40>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=6>0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}6 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}|=20>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=40>0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is positive-definite.

- Statement III is true. Since the matrix $A$ is positive-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local minimum of $f.$

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈3+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${a}_{11}=-2$ and $det(A)=-7$
- **II.** $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite
- **III.** $a$ is a saddle point of $f$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, let's recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-2$ and

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}|=-7.
$$

- Statement II is true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-2<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}|=-7<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite.

- Statement III is true. Since the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} {:db/id 17592186367888 :question/id #uuid "61ffb698-9cc2-5e02-b6d9-afec7d1f3422" :question/math-academy-id "q-163790" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "79848729-40e3-58f8-aead-25a4bf9f91ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468960} {:answer/id #uuid "bdf43adb-e00a-52d6-9171-6bb57f6c2393" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468961}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468960} :answer-field/id #uuid "6a2e7e84-4d50-5f18-bf38-f3d4119b4f61" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470092} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e1aeab25-5623-5fb1-a33c-8659586a7265" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468962} {:answer/id #uuid "000a5f85-f437-53f8-913c-2f859328fe33" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468963}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468962} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ea7aae1-f019-57b9-9bd5-f09302e71e14" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470093} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9e948e36-b6c1-5434-958f-e2bbe1ea693a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186468964} {:answer/id #uuid "5f6e86d7-eddf-593d-8716-1c788f8c5e9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186468965}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186468965} :answer-field/id #uuid "431cae4d-364e-588f-aeb2-fee9cea68018" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186470094}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{3}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈-7+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-5 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $det(A)>0$
- **II.** $A$ is positive-definite
- **III.** $a$ is a local maximum of $f$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -4\end{aligned}|+4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5(11)-2(-4)+4(10) \\  & =-7<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-5<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|=11>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-7<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is negative-definite.

- Statement III is true. Since the matrix $A$ is negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186434754 :question/id #uuid "5ec0f059-837e-5e3d-9bb4-8d292f2af4e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163781"} {:db/id 17592186434755 - The global maximum of a function is the largest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

17592186049676 :topic/id #uuid "0a177390-6525-5d0c-8721-f7f75db39408" :topic/math-academy-id 1945} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

One way is to consider the Taylor expansion of $f$ about $\mathbf{a}{:}$

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots
$$

Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a stationary point, we have $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T.$ This gives

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots.
$$

Let's assume that $\mathbf x$ is close to $\mathbf a,$ $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0,$ and that the terms of cubic order and higher are sufficiently small. Then, we have

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}).
$$

Recall that $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is an $n \times n$ *symmetric* matrix. Thus, the term

$$
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

is a *quadratic form*.

Therefore, we note the following:

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, this quadratic form is always positive, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) > 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) > f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *minimum*.

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, this quadratic form is always negative, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) < 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) < f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *maximum.*

- If this quadratic form is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point.

The assumption $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0$ is important. If $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) =0,$ then the quadratic form is zero along some line through $\mathbf a$ or zero *everywhere* in a neighborhood of $\mathbf a.$ In such cases, we cannot ignore the higher-order terms and must use another method to classify the critical point.

In the work that follows, we will only consider cases where $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3cedcd0c-77c7-5789-b76d-7ae3307c237b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4263 :tutorial/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Taylor Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f3f90cb9-acd8-5630-859d-3bd37e502189" :step/math-academy-id 25915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125645}} {:db/id 17592186125486 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125817 :tutorial/content "Recall that the *derivative* of a multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by the matrix

![](images/b5/b5dfe5fbad89ef3c6231dafe40d719be1faf007f782342abd6475756eda97b1e.svg)

Analogously with functions of one variable, we have the following definitions:

- A point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is a **critical point** of $f$ if $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ or does not exist.

- Critical points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ are known as **stationary points.**

The local extrema of a function $f$ occur at the critical points. So, we can find the local extrema of $f$ by determining the stationary points *and* the points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ does not exist and classify them accordingly (we'll discuss how to do this shortly). 

Not all of the solutions of $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ give rise to local extrema! Solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ that *do not* give rise to local extreme values are called **saddle points**.

For example, consider the hyperbolic paraboloid 

$$
z = f(x,y) = y^2-x^2
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/ce/cea092da684db6b055c78369fcb987c3577a027ef0d8f03d598e115e85775ff5.png)

It's easy to check that $\boldsymbol f'(0,0) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and so $(0,0)$ is a stationary point of $f.$ This point is a saddle point. Note that the surface curves up in one direction (the red curve) and down in a different direction (the green curve), resembling a horse riding saddle.

In any neighborhood of a saddle point $\mathbf a,$ there are points $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}'$ such that $\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}'-\mathbf{a}$ are orthogonal and they satisfy

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf a) >0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad f(\mathbf{x}') - f(\mathbf a) <0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60d15795-6c7a-5ec9-806d-625f5d8c5c85" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4264 :tutorial/title "Saddle Points"} :step/id #uuid "42eecd67-0de9-5101-84f7-5ef560683d60" 44846 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125486}} {:db/id 17592186125628 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125873 :tutorial/content "Now, recall the definition of local extrema for single-variable functions:

- A function $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

- A function $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

On the function's graph, a local minimum is the lowest point of a valley, and a local maximum is the highest point of a peak.

![](images/ba/ba5be082363bd963514baa6b1a777f02098d53a3b0a80ddc2fad231e4669ebd7.png)

We can generalize the concept of local extrema to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ as follows:

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a local minimum at the point $\mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x}$ in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{a}.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a local maximum at the point $\mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x}$ in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{a}.$

In particular, for a function $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ local minima and maxima are the lowest points in valleys and highest points in peaks, respectively, in the graph $z=f(x,y)$ of the function.

![](images/74/74d04165fd3bd5cd24ae82351bbf840e7d549b272c3deea16671dbfcd40bc75a.png)

For the points $A$ and $B,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $A$ and $B$ are the lowest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local minima.

Similarly, for the points $C$ and $D,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $C$ and $D$ are the highest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local maxima.

**Note**: For the point $E,$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f(x_E,y_E) = f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ or $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$, the point $E$ satisfies the conditions for a local minimum *and* a local maximum.

Finally, the points $F$ and $G$ are neither local minima nor local maxima. Notice that any neighborhood of $F$ will contain both points that lie higher than $F$ and lower than $F$ on the graph (similarly, for the point $G$)." :tutorial/id #uuid "fc6789c5-925e-54f4-9a5a-bfb179e77937" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7752 :tutorial/title "Local Extrema of a Multivariable Function"} :step/id #uuid "086acac3-3967-5f92-bf6e-ae6524a36328" :step/math-academy-id 44870 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125626}} {:db/id 17592186125629 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124648 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124211 :question/id #uuid "94c54743-ba74-51c5-9c59-777125bb76f6" :question/math-academy-id "e-12465"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "233eab4c-ab17-53a8-ae03-f6f28ac78922" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048555} {:db/id 17592186048786} {:db/id 17592186048883}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124820} {:db/id 17592186124823} {:db/id 17592186284417} {:db/id 17592186284420} {:db/id 17592186284421} {:db/id 17592186284422} {:db/id 17592186367874} {:db/id 17592186401419} {:db/id 17592186434751} {:db/id 17592186434752} {:db/id 17592186434753} {:db/id 17592186434760}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "ab662d13-5448-5cfa-8e5b-f6bf4d245b75" :step/math-academy-id 44871 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125487}} {:db/id 17592186125630 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125874 :tutorial/content "Recall the following definitions for single-variable functions:

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global minimum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global maximum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

On the function's graph, the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points, respectively.

![](images/63/633526565293f480a6a5fc45b87a70d38e946ae0f72a925f0074776e201a43a4.png)

We can generalize this concept to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global minimum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global minimum** of the function, the smallest value the function attains on its domain.

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global maximum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global maximum** of the function, the largest value the function attains on its domain.

In particular, for a function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points on the graph $z=f(x,y),$ respectively.

![](images/de/de4cfc96fdce210430291999e5997f4a0c39ed1fbe63c3848b61508ca3f04114.png)

For the function shown above:

- The minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = -2,$ so the global minimum is $-2,$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,-1).$ Therefore the global minimum point is $(1,-1,-2).$

- Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d367e806-9c4c-5d98-bc43-97c56882eee8" :step/math-academy-id 44876 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125625}} {:db/id 17592186125645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125885 :tutorial/content "To summarize, the point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a stationary point of the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ if $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and we can classify $\mathbf{a}$ as follows:

- Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d367e806-9c4c-5d98-bc43-97c56882eee8" :step/math-academy-id 44876 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125625}} {:db/id 17592186125485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

One way is to consider the Taylor expansion of $f$ about $\mathbf{a}{:}$

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots
$$

Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a stationary point, we have $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T.$ This gives

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots.
$$

Let's assume that $\mathbf x$ is close to $\mathbf a,$ $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0,$ and that the terms of cubic order and higher are sufficiently small. Then, we have

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}).
$$

Recall that $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is an $n \times n$ *symmetric* matrix. Thus, the term

$$
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

is a *quadratic form*.

Therefore, we note the following:

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, this quadratic form is always positive, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) > 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) > f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *minimum*.

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, this quadratic form is always negative, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) < 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) < f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *maximum.*

- If this quadratic form is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point.

The assumption $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0$ is important. If $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) =0,$ then the quadratic form is zero along some line through $\mathbf a$ or zero *everywhere* in a neighborhood of $\mathbf a.$ In such cases, we cannot ignore the higher-order terms and must use another method to classify the critical point.

In the work that follows, we will only consider cases where $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3cedcd0c-77c7-5789-b76d-7ae3307c237b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4263 :tutorial/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Taylor Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f3f90cb9-acd8-5630-859d-3bd37e502189" :step/math-academy-id 25915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125645}} {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

Analogously with functions of one variable, we have the following definitions:

- A point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is a **critical point** of $f$ if $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ or does not exist.

- Critical points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ are known as **stationary points.**

The local extrema of a function $f$ occur at the critical points. So, we can find the local extrema of $f$ by determining the stationary points *and* the points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ does not exist and classify them accordingly (we'll discuss how to do this shortly). 

Not all of the solutions of $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ give rise to local extrema! Solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ that *do not* give rise to local extreme values are called **saddle points**.

For example, consider the hyperbolic paraboloid 

$$
z = f(x,y) = y^2-x^2
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/ce/cea092da684db6b055c78369fcb987c3577a027ef0d8f03d598e115e85775ff5.png)

It's easy to check that $\boldsymbol f'(0,0) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and so $(0,0)$ is a stationary point of $f.$ This point is a saddle point. Note that the surface curves up in one direction (the red curve) and down in a different direction (the green curve), resembling a horse riding saddle.

In any neighborhood of a saddle point $\mathbf a,$ there are points $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}'$ such that $\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}'-\mathbf{a}$ are orthogonal and they satisfy

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf a) >0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad f(\mathbf{x}') - f(\mathbf a) <0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60d15795-6c7a-5ec9-806d-625f5d8c5c85" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4264 :tutorial/title "Saddle Points"} :step/id #uuid "42eecd67-0de9-5101-84f7-5ef560683d60" :step/math-academy-id 25917 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125485}} {:db/id 17592186125817 :tutorial/content "Recall that the *derivative* of a multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by the matrix

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global minimum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global maximum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

On the function's graph, the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points, respectively.

![](images/63/633526565293f480a6a5fc45b87a70d38e946ae0f72a925f0074776e201a43a4.png)

We can generalize this concept to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global minimum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global minimum** of the function, the smallest value the function attains on its domain.

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global maximum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global maximum** of the function, the largest value the function attains on its domain.

In particular, for a function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points on the graph $z=f(x,y),$ respectively.

![](images/de/de4cfc96fdce210430291999e5997f4a0c39ed1fbe63c3848b61508ca3f04114.png)

For the function shown above:

- The minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = -2,$ so the global minimum is $-2,$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,-1).$ Therefore the global minimum point is $(1,-1,-2).$

- Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125885 :tutorial/content "To summarize, the point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a stationary point of the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ if $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and we can classify $\mathbf{a}$ as follows:

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a local minimum

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a local maximum

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point" :tutorial/id #uuid "ab23ca4b-1bff-5c96-a4d2-62b72b8adff2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7852 :tutorial/title "A Summary of Key Results"} {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186445202} :activity/id #uuid "632f0c8c-4357-5396-aad3-4401d3471d8c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049676 :topic/id #uuid "0a177390-6525-5d0c-8721-f7f75db39408" :topic/math-academy-id 1945} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186445199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186367874 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "99f22169-b8a2-5fb3-aca1-3e5599415ad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local maximum" :db/id 17592186367876} {:answer/id #uuid "abbaa7f2-5259-5b5a-bebd-07f255b181e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "inconclusive" :db/id 17592186367877} {:answer/id #uuid "f674340e-9bc4-5748-9997-f0404db95ca2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "not a critical point" :db/id 17592186367878} {:answer/id #uuid "383240c1-34bf-5387-adaf-b9355e4cf27e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local minimum" :db/id 17592186367879} {:answer/id #uuid "0e483432-9f14-537e-b0dd-61a175cc1645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "saddle point" :db/id 17592186367880}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367876} :answer-field/id #uuid "be669623-0526-55a8-9e58-06217378cfec" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367875}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1f0502ee-0a83-5915-919b-cb8a0333bfec" :question/math-academy-id "q-163775" :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}(x-a).
$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-3<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-9<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. $$
f(x)≈1+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & -6\end{bmatrix}(x-a).
$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-3<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-9<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. Therefore, $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$"} :step/id #uuid "40399da2-21fd-5f08-bac2-f30a1d0cf8b3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445203}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid - The global minimum of a function is the smallest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global minimum.

- A global minimum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global minimum. There can be zero, one, or many global minimum points.

For our function, the minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y)=-2.$ Therefore, the global minimum is $-2.$ The function reaches this value when $(x,y)=(1,1),$ so the global minimum point is $(1,1,-2).$

The graph $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. What are the global maximum points of the function?" :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global maximum of a function is the largest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

- A global maximum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global maximum. There can be zero, one, or many global maximum points.

For our function, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y)=3.$ Therefore, the global maximum is $3.$ The function reaches this value when $(x,y)=(-2,1),$ so the global maximum point is $(-2,1,3).$

$$
