a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,P=\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}{p}_{11} & {p}_{12} & {p}_{13} \\ {p}_{21} & {p}_{22} & {p}_{23} \\ {p}_{31} & {p}_{32} & {p}_{33}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that the vector $a$ above spans ${S}^{⊥},$ and that $P$ is the orthogonal projection matrix of ${R}^{3}$ onto the subspace $S$, what is the value of ${p}_{12}+{p}_{33}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the orthogonal projection matrix onto ${S}^{⊥}=\text{Span}\{a\}.$

Using the formula for the orthogonal projection matrix

$$
{P}_{{S}^{⊥}}=a({a}^{T}\,a)^{-1}{a}^{T},
$$

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{([\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={6}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that ${P}_{S}+{P}_{{S}^{⊥}}=I.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S} & =I-{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 5 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, ${p}_{12}+{p}_{33}=1+2=3.$"} :step/id #uuid "40a5ccf0-6aa1-5ea7-b903-ef49b53ecb1a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186554655}} {:db/id 17592186554685 :step/content {:db/id 17592186554561 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26616721-c1c2-5d9f-b10a-79047fee470c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186553939} {:answer/id #uuid "5645af54-a6c4-584e-8e27-fcde9bec94bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186554036} {:answer/id #uuid "8dbf19db-8c12-56d5-93cb-c6a8e4c35f89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186554171} {:answer/id #uuid "95678053-edd8-5ce0-accb-5d3d57aea431" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186554199} {:answer/id #uuid "ac5c093f-adcb-5278-a948-2600588e194d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186554253}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554171} :answer-field/id #uuid "f95e685a-8719-5a28-8f48-34b22e58d837" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554535}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3561f664-6b98-59a1-983b-c026ed37b09d" :question/math-academy-id "q-95340" :question/problem "$$

III. $A$ is an orthogonal projection matrix" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $Q$ is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if ${Q}^{2}=Q$ and ${Q}^{T}=Q.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${A}^{T}=A.$

- Statement II is false. Indeed, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}20 & 10 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{20}{9} & \frac{10}{9} \\ \frac{10}{9} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false since not both statements I and II are true.

#uuid "90216c0e-e4a5-5933-86e0-58d218939e29" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Index of a Term Given the Recursive Formula"}] :question/problem "What is the index of the term $16$ for the geometric sequence below?

$a_{n+1} = 2 a_n \quad a_1 = \dfrac{1}{4},\quad n\geq 1$" :question/worked-solution "This geometric sequence is given as a recurrence relation, i.e.,

$$
a_{n+1} = {\color{blue}r} \cdot a_n
$$

Therefore,

$$
a_1 = \dfrac{1}{4}, \quad {\color{blue}r}=2
$$

We're interested in finding $n$ such that $a_n = 16$. Using the formula for the $n$th term, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\
16 &= \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
2^{4} &= \frac{1}{2^{2}} \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
2^{6} &= 2^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the exponents gives:

$$
6 = n - 1\quad \Longrightarrow \quad n = 7
$$

$32$?" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given that $a_4=8$, we can use the formula for the $n$th term to solve for $r$, as follows:

$$

\end{aligned}
$$

$$
a_{n} = 1 \cdot 2^{n - 1}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= 1 \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
32 &= 2^{n - 1} \\
2^{5} &= 2^{n - 1} \\
5 &= n - 1 \\
6 &= n
\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $a_2=24$ and $a_5=3$, so we can find the common ratio using a formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{n - m} &= \frac{a_{n}}{a_{m}} \\
r^{5 - 2} &= \frac{a_{5}}{a_{2}} \\
r^{5 - 2} &= \frac{3}{24} \\
r^{3} &= \frac{1}{8} \\
r^{3} &= (\frac{1}{2})^{3} \\
r &= \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we know the common ratio is

$$
r=\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

, we can use the same formula to solve for the value of $k$ such that $a_k=12$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{n - m} &= \frac{a_{n}}{a_{m}} \\
r^{k - 2} &= \frac{a_{k}}{a_{2}} \\
(\frac{1}{2})^{k - 2} &= \frac{12}{24} \\
(\frac{1}{2})^{k - 2} &= \frac{1}{2} \\
(\frac{1}{2})^{k - 2} &= (\frac{1}{2})^{1} \\
k - 2 &= 1 \\
k &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049083} {:db/id 17592186078895 :question/id #uuid "09e41287-56b1-51c2-8364-6f01662d04ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-39738"} {:db/id 17592186079114 :question/id #uuid "cf5edc3d-d94c-5428-950a-0bf9dfc9cd27" :question/math-academy-id "q-5418" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186078565 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aaa87d67-d9df-5bbb-b98e-00d72d16fe7f" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Index of a Particular Term When the First Term is Unknown"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a4f9efab-c17e-5931-874b-5cb792746161" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186077463} {:answer/id #uuid "be4a1d02-6c11-53d8-bb2a-bbddaa5995c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186077464} {:answer/id #uuid "c36b5c65-40b1-552d-862a-de2a63efc6f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186077465} {:answer/id #uuid "f504c69c-388e-57d9-a607-08dc26fde645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186077466} {:answer/id #uuid "08c4a91e-aadd-53e9-b0dc-ff0807a0ad64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186077467}] :answer-field/id #uuid "224c0fd0-9ee8-5e0e-b223-2902f04f8b4a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186077462}] :question/problem "Given that a positive geometric sequence has

using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

to compute the terms of a geometric sequence, we can also use it to compute the index of a desired term in a geometric sequence.

To illustrate, suppose we're given the geometric sequence

$$
3, \: 6, \: 12, \: \ldots, \:96, \ldots
$$

that has the first term $a_1=3$ and the common ratio $r=2$. What index gives the term $96$? In other words, what value of $n$ gives $a_n=96$?

We can construct the formula for the $n$th term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\
&= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the value of $n$ that gives $a_n=96$, we can use the formula for the $n$th term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
96 &= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
32 &= 2^{n - 1} \\
2^{5} &= 2^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the exponents gives:

$$
5 = n - 1\quad \Longrightarrow \quad n = 6
$$

Therefore, $96$ is the $6$th term of the sequence." :tutorial/id #uuid "77450737-c02f-5751-b70b-0b387def70eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1672 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fbfa3bf3-20c5-5d4d-a7dd-74222bd4805e" :step/math-academy-id 4734 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079314}} {:db/id 17592186079510 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078564 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078205 :question/id #uuid "426f52d9-ad0e-5ef3-a545-78315ea02c0e" :question/math-academy-id "e-1514"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d47c0304-a438-5444-9add-5e4f61acbbcd" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186079113} {:db/id 17592186079126}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Index of a Term Given the First Term and Another Term"} :step/id #uuid "a4bf9b19-3f3a-5399-8f55-c85f6684f07d" :step/math-academy-id 4735 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079313}} {:db/id 17592186079511 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078565 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078206 :question/id #uuid "e3fed3e8-9bc6-558d-a426-96006871a20d" :question/math-academy-id "e-1516"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aaa87d67-d9df-5bbb-b98e-00d72d16fe7f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049083}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078895} {:db/id 17592186079114}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Index of a Particular Term When the First Term is Unknown"} :step/id #uuid "a73a35bf-c363-53aa-a8e5-abf04854ae43" :step/math-academy-id 4741}] :activity/title "Determining Indexes of Terms in Geometric Sequences" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186078698} {:db/id 17592186079509 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079627 :tutorial/content "In addition to using the formula

to compute the terms of a geometric sequence, we can also use it to compute the index of a desired term in a geometric sequence.

$$
3, \: 6, \: 12, \: \ldots, \:96, \ldots

that has the first term $a_1=3$ and the common ratio $r=2$. What index gives the term $96$? In other words, what value of $n$ gives $a_n=96$?

We can construct the formula for the $n$th term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\

:tutorial/content "In addition to using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

to compute the terms of a geometric sequence, we can also use it to compute the index of a desired term in a geometric sequence.

To illustrate, suppose we're given the geometric sequence

$$
3, \: 6, \: 12, \: \ldots, \:96, \ldots
$$

that has the first term $a_1=3$ and the common ratio $r=2$. What index gives the term $96$? In other words, what value of $n$ gives $a_n=96$?

We can construct the formula for the $n$th term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= a_{1} \cdot r^{n - 1} \\
&= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the value of $n$ that gives $a_n=96$, we can use the formula for the $n$th term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
96 &= 3 \cdot 2^{n - 1} \\
32 &= 2^{n - 1} \\
2^{5} &= 2^{n - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the exponents gives:

$$
5 = n - 1\quad \Longrightarrow \quad n = 6
$$

Therefore, $96$ is the $6$th term of the sequence." :tutorial/id #uuid "77450737-c02f-5751-b70b-0b387def70eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1672 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186050680 To do this, we solve each inequality individually and then compute the union of the two solutions.

We start by solving $4x+2 < 6\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2 & <6 \\ 4x & <4 \\ x & <1\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/0d/0d36b8e68d9fd0b33b255502860481eeb525b60382029b17434bfb072cc39da2.png)

Then, we solve $2x \geq 8\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & \ge 8 \\ x & \ge 4\end{aligned}

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](images/5c/5c60839a626f2ba8a0fe4a24f4011af0fa52c00d79fbf80039bcfdbdf0a612c7.png)

Thus, the final solution is $x < 1$ or $x \geq 4.$ We can write this using interval notation as

$$
(-\infty, 1) \cup [4,\infty).

Quadratic Curve Type"}] :question/problem "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation
![](images/3b/3bf74b3f4c11508b9daa66464cc451933f5637c22ffeaaae303378fca2571893.png)
and the curve $\mathcal C,$ defined as

$$
\mathcal C:\: 2x_1^2+6x_1x_2+ 2x_2^2 -2x_1+2x_2 =7 .
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2+6x_1x_2+2x_2^2$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $5y_1^2-y_2^2,$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $\mathcal C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\: \underbrace{ 2x_1^2+6x_1x_2+2x_2^2}_{Q(\mathbf{x})} -2x_1+2x_2 =7
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

![](images/78/783b32a7595534982e5fb057c049081564807b9d47988670c7d30058fb3900a0.png)

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(\mathbf x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $\mathcal C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2})+2(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2}) & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable $y_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2} & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}) & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2})+2 & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-({y}_{2}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}{y}_{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2})+(\sqrt{2})^{2} & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-\sqrt{2})}^{2}+2 & =7 \\ 5{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-\sqrt{2})}^{2} & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}-\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-\sqrt{2})}^{2} & =5 \\ 5{z}_{1}^{2}-{z}_{2}^{2} & =5 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}-\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This represents a hyperbola with semiaxes $1$ and $\sqrt5.$"} {:db/id 17592186048300} {:db/id 17592186172620 :question/id #uuid "99b32268-480f-53e7-a19a-fe74688e6626" :question/math-academy-id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-26.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-26
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2} & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})-2\sqrt{5}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2}) & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2} & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2} & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+({y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2}+25)-25 & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}-5)}^{2}-25 & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}-5)}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}-5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{z}_{1}^{2}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =-1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}})^{2}}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This defines an empty set, also called an imaginary ellipse. Notice that the left-hand side is non-negative for all ${z}_{1}$ and ${z}_{2},$ while the right-hand side is negative."} {:db/id 17592186366615 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=40.
$$

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=40
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly: 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}14{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}+3\sqrt{10}{x}_{2} & =40 \\ 15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2}+\sqrt{10}(-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2})+3\sqrt{10}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2}) & =40 \\ 15{y}_{1}^{2}+5{y}_{2}^{2}+10{y}_{2} & =40 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2} & =8 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+({y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{2}+1) & =8+1 \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}+1)}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}+1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}_{1}^{2}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =9 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This represents an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt{3}$ and $3.$"} {:db/id 17592186366622 :question/id #uuid "52bc4c30-7a1f-5187-9432-fbae24061f19" :question/math-academy-id "q-95395"} {:db/id "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}-6\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=0.
$$

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $10{y}_{1}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,{{{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}+2\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}-6\sqrt{10}{x}_{2}=0
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly: 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}+2\sqrt{10}{x}_{1}-6\sqrt{10}{x}_{2} & =0 \\ 10{y}_{1}^{2}+2\sqrt{10}(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2})-6\sqrt{10}(\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{y}_{2}) & =0 \\ 10{y}_{1}^{2}-20{y}_{1} & =0 \\ {y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1} & =0 \\ ({y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}+1)-1 & =0 \\ {({y}_{1}-1)}^{2}-1 & =0 \\ {({y}_{1}-1)}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
{z}_{1}={y}_{1}-1,
$$

we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}_{1}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

which represents the pair of parallel lines  ${z}_{1}=1$ and ${z}_{1}=-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186550002 :question/id #uuid "d27201ee-27d4-58dc-b2ff-368cd1c77509" :question/math-academy-id "q-140569"} {:db/id 17592186172029 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171835 :question/id #uuid "c03c6fbb-176a-5f30-b928-73908cb93277" :question/math-academy-id "e-8380"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7a6bbb34-a43f-5e16-8a24-25c0d6970a38" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048366} {:db/id 17592186049233} {:db/id 17592186049456}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172624 :question/id #uuid "7fe38749-b027-5e25-83ce-123ba8294cb8" :question/math-academy-id "q-95701"} {:db/id 17592186172625 :question/id #uuid "098d9a26-30b9-593f-93e1-d543e66fd2ef" :question/math-academy-id "q-95703"} {:db/id 17592186365010 :question/id #uuid "d7ec5e81-6115-5881-b6f7-16bb9226da5a" :question/math-academy-id "q-140554"} {:db/id 17592186366704 :question/id #uuid "b9c400a7-1475-5262-8bba-899ae2d20b23" :question/math-academy-id "q-95882"} {:db/id 17592186366711 :question/id #uuid "794275ca-3602-5fb3-b396-bcfd2452a9d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-95890"} {:db/id 17592186366718 :question/id #uuid "66610d66-38e7-5d9e-b883-9467a5f6ad73" :question/math-academy-id "q-95897"}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Quadratic Curve Type From Its Reduced Equation: No Cross-Product Term"} {:db/id 17592186171835 :question/id #uuid "c03c6fbb-176a-5f30-b928-73908cb93277" :question/math-academy-id "e-8380" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186172029 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7a6bbb34-a43f-5e16-8a24-25c0d6970a38" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Quadratic Curve Type From Its Reduced Equation: No Cross-Product Term"}] :question/problem "Which of the following equations define a non-empty set of points in the ![](images/a4/a49d63b985288c12f1f2e6494534c6d69a52b52cb19b15ff716c5893aaaadbf8.png)-plane?

$$
3x_1^2 + 2x_1 - x_2 =\dfrac{5}{3}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square for the variable $x_1\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3({x}_{1}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1})-{x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3({x}_{1}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{x}_{1}+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2})-{x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3{({x}_{1}+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-3{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3{({x}_{1}+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{x}_{2} & =\frac{5}{3} \\ 3{({x}_{1}+\frac{1}{3})}^{2} & ={x}_{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &={x}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}, \\ {y}_{2} &={x}_{2}+2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}_{1}^{2} & ={y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

[{:db/id 17592186172885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173152 :tutorial/content "The general equation of a second order (quadratic) curve is an expression of the form

$$\alpha_{11}x_1^2+2\alpha_{12}x_1x_2 + \alpha_{22}x_2^2 + 2\alpha_{13}x_1+ 2\alpha_{23}x_2 +\alpha_{33}=0,$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are variables, and $\alpha_{ij} \in \Bbb R$ for all $1\leq i,j \leq 3.$

For example,

$$3x_1^2-x_1x_2-5x_2^2+5x_2 - 1 = 0$$

is a general quadratic curve." :tutorial/id #uuid "2d9b3527-1999-5169-affa-96a37f99fb01" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5004 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8cf7cde9-4168-5bb5-a77b-f1c02aa56436" :step/math-academy-id 31225 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172919}} {:db/id 17592186172886 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172028 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171834 :question/id #uuid "1ecd84f8-5157-595a-93b6-a865acaa53d9" :question/math-academy-id "e-8378"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "26871e46-51ca-5680-a064-bcee4ac984fd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048300}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172620} {:db/id 17592186172621} {:db/id 17592186366615} {:db/id 17592186366622} {:db/id 17592186366629} {:db/id 17592186381104} {:db/id 17592186404801} {:db/id 17592186404808} {:db/id 17592186550002}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Quadratic Curve Type"} :step/id #uuid "b2f2a127-b40d-5b8f-ba64-4a1cad0e08c9" :step/math-academy-id 31226} {:db/id 17592186172887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173153 :tutorial/content "In general, the cross-term of a quadratic equation can be eliminated by an orthogonal change of variables. That is, one of the kind $$\mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y} ,$$ where the columns of $P$ form an orthonormal eigenbasis for the corresponding quadratic form's matrix.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a plane curve defined as

$$\mathcal C:\: 2x_1x_2 -2\sqrt2x_1+2\sqrt2x_2 =8.$$

How do we determine the type of our curve?

Notice that the quadratic form $2x_1x_2$ can be reduced to canonical form $y_1^2-y_2^2$ using the change of variables $$\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.$$

First, let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.$$

We know that this change of variables reduces the corresponding quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = 2x_1x_2$ to its canonical form. Indeed, performing the change of variables on $\mathcal C,$ gives

$$\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=8\,⟹\,{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+4{y}_{2}=8,\end{aligned}$$ and, by completing the square for the variable $y_2$, we get the equation

$$\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-2)}^{2} & =4.\end{aligned}$$

The graph of the resulting equation in the $y_1,y_2$ variables is the following.

![](images/d5/d532f5207a9d518f92024c86689285834b86c961d0f647d6ee99ad6dd9c7c329.png)

Notice that we can write down the change-of-variables matrix as $$\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}{45}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{45}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{45}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{45}^{∘}\end{bmatrix},$$ which is a rotation matrix. Looking at the diagram above, we see that going from one coordinate system to another can be viewed as a rotation of our axes by $45^\circ.$

**Watch out!** In general, this action is an orthogonal transformation (it can be a rotation, a reflection, or a combination of such transformations).

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}-2,\end{aligned}\right.$$

we get the following:

$$\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-2)}^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}$$

This (standard) equation represents a hyperbola in which both semiaxes are equal to $2.$

In the diagram below we represent the curve in the $z_1,z_2$ variables.

![](images/c3/c36709f752bd9c319662e7e2150c54031cc8fb3934be37711c65e7a7668829ca.png)

Looking at the diagram above, we see that in the final step we simply translated our system by $(0,2)$ in $y$-coordinates.

**Note:** Finding the simplest equation of a quadratic curve can be viewed as the following series of steps:

- **Step 1**. We eliminate the cross-term by reducing the quadratic part to canonical form. Geometrically, this is equivalent to an orthogonal transformation of our coordinate system.
- **Step 2**. We eliminate the linear terms by completing the squares. Geometrically, this is equivalent to a translation of our coordinate system." :tutorial/id #uuid "cd5dde1f-7d5c-58d9-8674-6bf984a51d0d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5005 :tutorial/title "Classifying a "Identifying a Quadratic Curve Type: No Cross-Product Term"} :step/id #uuid "8393be76-0567-5bf7-bd97-bfad1ef56506" :step/math-academy-id 31230 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172887}} {:db/id 17592186172891 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173155 :tutorial/content "A quadratic equation with no cross-terms can be rewritten in standard form by completing the square. Let's see how this is done in the following example.

Suppose we are given the equation

$$2x_1^2+x_2^2 - 4x_1 + 4x_2 = 2,$$

what type of curve does it represent?

First, we complete the squares for the variables $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-4{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1})+({x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{2}) & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}+1-1)+({x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{2}+4-4) & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}-1)^{2}-2+({x}_{2}+2)^{2}-4 & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}-1)^{2}+({x}_{2}+2)^{2} & =8\end{aligned}$$

Now, performing the change of variables

$$\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &={x}_{1}-1, \\ {y}_{2} &={x}_{2}+2,\end{aligned}\right.$$

we get the following equation in standard form:

$$\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{8} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{8})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}$$

This represents an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $\sqrt{8}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd1f3565-37df-5db7-aa06-a573b6b58f8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5015 :tutorial/title "Classifying a Quadratic Curve That Does Not Contain a Cross-Product Term"} :step/id #uuid "ea16c9e4-6358-52d5-9437-e5c11b9cdeec" :step/math-academy-id 31358 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172889}} {:db/id 17592186172919 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173165 :tutorial/content "There are three basic so-called *non-degenerate quadratic curves*:

| Standard Equation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=1$ | Ellipse |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=1$ | Hyperbola |
| $x_2^2= 2px_1$ | Parabola |" :tutorial/id #uuid "31519439-ac97-5940-b01b-de36561f9618" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5129 :tutorial/title "Non-Degenerate Quadratic Curves"} :step/id #uuid "1e64c954-a22d-5a07-9a29-b00dae41d7a4" :step/math-academy-id 32209 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172920}} {:db/id 17592186172920 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173166 :tutorial/content "There are also a few so-called *degenerate (real) quadratic curves:*

| Standard Equation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ | Pair of<br> intersecting lines |
| ${x_i^2}=a^2$ | Pair of <br> parallel lines |
| ${x_i^2}=0$ | Pair of <br> coincident lines |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ | Single point |

Let's see why these equations define the described curves:

- $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ is equivalent to $(bx_1 - ax_2)(bx_1 + ax_2)=0$ which in turn gives equations of two lines $bx_1 - ax_2=0$ and $bx_1 + ax_2=0$ intersecting at the origin.
- ${x_i^2}=a^2$ is equivalent to $(x_i - a)(x_i + a)=0$ which in turn gives equations of two parallel lines $x_i =a$ and $x_i=-a.$
- ${x_i^2}=0$ gives equations of two coincident lines $x_i =0$ and $-x_i=0.$
- $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ is equivalent to $b^2x_1^2+a^2x_2^2=0$ which in turn gives a single point, the origin, since the sum of two squares is $0$ if and only if both squares are $0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7fa5c07c-714f-555e-9253-e8c6b56484e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5130 :tutorial/title "Degenerate (Real) Quadratic Curves"} :step/id #uuid "e4b30b5f-3e46-516c-bdb2-28d2099fba5a" :step/math-academy-id 32210 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172921}} {:db/id 17592186172921 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173167 :tutorial/content "Finally, some quadratic equations might define an *empty set* (or so-called *imaginary curve*):

| Standard Equation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=-1$ | Imaginary ellipse |
| $x_i^2=-a^2$ | Pair of imaginary<br> parallel lines |

Let's see why these equations define the described curves:

- Although there are no real solutions, the equation $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2} = -1,$ which is equivalent to $\dfrac{x_1^2}{(a\textrm{i})^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{(b\textrm{i})^2} = 1,$ has imaginary solutions, so we could interpret this as an imaginary ellipse.
- Although there are no real solutions, the equation ${x_i^2}=-a^2$ is equivalent to $(x_i - a\textrm{i})(x_i + a\textrm{i})=0$ which in turn gives equations of two imaginary parallel lines $x_i =a\textrm{i}$ and $x_i=-a\textrm{i}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "81eb37e3-202d-5934-93ce-8534c3ffc1a0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5131 :tutorial/title "Empty Sets"} :step/id #uuid "980cb0f2-0635-5e7b-926e-f8cbd302bf7b" :step/math-academy-id 32211 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172888}}] :activity/title "Classifying Quadratic Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172167} {:db/id 17592186172885 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173152 :tutorial/content "The general equation of a second order (quadratic) curve is an expression of the form

$$\alpha_{11}x_1^2+2\alpha_{12}x_1x_2 + \alpha_{22}x_2^2 + 2\alpha_{13}x_1+ 2\alpha_{23}x_2 +\alpha_{33}=0,$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are variables, and $\alpha_{ij} \in \Bbb R$ for all $1\leq i,j \leq 3.$

For example,

$$3x_1^2-x_1x_2-5x_2^2+5x_2 - 1 = 0$$

is a general quadratic curve." :tutorial/id #uuid "2d9b3527-1999-5169-affa-96a37f99fb01" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5004 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8cf7cde9-4168-5bb5-a77b-f1c02aa56436" :step/math-academy-id 31225 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172919}} {:db/id 17592186173152 :tutorial/content "The general equation of a second order (quadratic) curve is an expression of the form

That is, one of the kind $$\mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y} ,$$ where the columns of $P$ form an orthonormal eigenbasis for the corresponding quadratic form's matrix.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a plane curve defined as

$$\mathcal C:\: 2x_1x_2 -2\sqrt2x_1+2\sqrt2x_2 =8.$$

How do we determine the type of our curve?

Notice that the quadratic form $2x_1x_2$ can be reduced to canonical form $y_1^2-y_2^2$ using the change of variables $$\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.$$

First, let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.$$

We know that this change of variables reduces the corresponding quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = 2x_1x_2$ to its canonical form. Indeed, performing the change of variables on $\mathcal C,$ gives

$$\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=8\,⟹\,{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}+4{y}_{2}=8,\end{aligned}$$ and, by completing the square for the variable $y_2$, we get the equation

$$\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-2)}^{2} & =4.\end{aligned}$$

The graph of the resulting equation in the $y_1,y_2$ variables is the following.

![](images/d5/d532f5207a9d518f92024c86689285834b86c961d0f647d6ee99ad6dd9c7c329.png)

Notice that we can write down the change-of-variables matrix as $$\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}{45}^{∘} & -\operatorname{sin}{45}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}{45}^{∘} & \operatorname{cos}{45}^{∘}\end{bmatrix},$$ which is a rotation matrix. Looking at the diagram above, we see that going from one coordinate system to another can be viewed as a rotation of our axes by $45^\circ.$

**Watch out!** In general, this action is an orthogonal transformation (it can be a rotation, a reflection, or a combination of such transformations).

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}-2,\end{aligned}\right.$$

we get the following:

$$\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2}-{({y}_{2}-2)}^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{{z}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}$$

This (standard) equation represents a hyperbola in which both semiaxes are equal to $2.$

In the diagram below we represent the curve in the $z_1,z_2$ variables.

![](images/c3/c36709f752bd9c319662e7e2150c54031cc8fb3934be37711c65e7a7668829ca.png)

Looking at the diagram above, we see that in the final step we simply translated our system by $(0,2)$ in $y$-coordinates.

**Note:** Finding the simplest equation of a quadratic curve can be viewed as the following series of steps:

- **Step 1**. We eliminate the cross-term by reducing the quadratic part to canonical form. Geometrically, this is equivalent to an orthogonal transformation of our coordinate system.
- **Step 2**. We eliminate the linear terms by completing the squares. Geometrically, this is equivalent to a translation of our coordinate system." :tutorial/id #uuid "cd5dde1f-7d5c-58d9-8674-6bf984a51d0d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5005 :tutorial/title "Classifying a General Quadratic Curve"} :step/id #uuid "e347e125-d8fa-58ef-8dc4-81fc67d191f3" :step/math-academy-id 31227 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172886}} {:db/id 17592186173153 :tutorial/content "In general, the cross-term of a quadratic equation can be eliminated by an orthogonal change of variables. Let's see how this is done in the following example.

Suppose we are given the equation

$$2x_1^2+x_2^2 - 4x_1 + 4x_2 = 2,$$

what type of curve does it represent?

First, we complete the squares for the variables $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-4{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1})+({x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{2}) & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}+1-1)+({x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{2}+4-4) & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}-1)^{2}-2+({x}_{2}+2)^{2}-4 & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}-1)^{2}+({x}_{2}+2)^{2} & =8\end{aligned}$$

Now, performing the change of variables

$$\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &={x}_{1}-1, \\ {y}_{2} &={x}_{2}+2,\end{aligned}\right.$$

we get the following equation in standard form:

$$\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{8} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{8})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}$$

This represents an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $\sqrt{8}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd1f3565-37df-5db7-aa06-a573b6b58f8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5015 :tutorial/title "Classifying a Quadratic Curve That Does Not Contain a Cross-Product Term"} :step/id #uuid "ea16c9e4-6358-52d5-9437-e5c11b9cdeec" :step/math-academy-id 31358 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172889}} {:db/id 17592186172889 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172030 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171836 :question/id #uuid "58f6a3e7-e867-576a-ad84-0debbbc38d90" :question/math-academy-id "e-8381"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "49b74a69-2c2c-5286-a987-fee946fd48b6" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186051078}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172622} {:db/id 17592186172623} {:db/id 17592186365017} {:db/id 17592186366725} {:db/id 17592186366732} {:db/id 17592186382614} {:db/id 17592186400888} {:db/id 17592186404857} {:db/id 17592186404864} {:db/id 17592186404871}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Quadratic Curve Type: No Cross-Product Term"} :step/id #uuid "8393be76-0567-5bf7-bd97-bfad1ef56506" :step/math-academy-id 31230 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172887}} {:db/id 17592186173155 :tutorial/content "A quadratic equation with no cross-terms can be rewritten in standard form by completing the square. Let's see how this is done in the following example.

Suppose we are given the equation

$$2x_1^2+x_2^2 - 4x_1 + 4x_2 = 2,$$

what type of curve does it represent?

First, we complete the squares for the variables $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-4{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1})+({x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{2}) & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}+1-1)+({x}_{2}^{2}+4{x}_{2}+4-4) & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}-1)^{2}-2+({x}_{2}+2)^{2}-4 & =2 \\ 2({x}_{1}-1)^{2}+({x}_{2}+2)^{2} & =8\end{aligned}$$

Now, performing the change of variables

$$\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &={x}_{1}-1, \\ {y}_{2} &={x}_{2}+2,\end{aligned}\right.$$

we get the following equation in standard form:

$$\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} & =8 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{8} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{8})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}$$

This represents an ellipse with semiaxes $2$ and $\sqrt{8}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd1f3565-37df-5db7-aa06-a573b6b58f8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5015 :tutorial/title "Classifying a Quadratic Curve That Does Not Contain a Cross-Product Term"} {:db/id 17592186173165 :tutorial/content "There are three basic so-called *non-degenerate quadratic curves*:

| Standard Equation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=1$ | Ellipse |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=1$ | Hyperbola |
| $x_2^2= 2px_1$ | Parabola |" :tutorial/id #uuid "31519439-ac97-5940-b01b-de36561f9618" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5129 :tutorial/title "Non-Degenerate Quadratic Curves"} {:db/id 17592186172920 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173166 :tutorial/content "There are also a few so-called *degenerate (real) quadratic curves:*

| Standard Equation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ | Pair of<br> intersecting lines |
| ${x_i^2}=a^2$ | Pair of <br> parallel lines |
| ${x_i^2}=0$ | Pair of <br> coincident lines |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ | Single point |

Let's see why these equations define the described curves:

- $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ is equivalent to $(bx_1 - ax_2)(bx_1 + ax_2)=0$ which in turn gives equations of two lines $bx_1 - ax_2=0$ and $bx_1 + ax_2=0$ intersecting at the origin.
- ${x_i^2}=a^2$ is equivalent to $(x_i - a)(x_i + a)=0$ which in turn gives equations of two parallel lines $x_i =a$ and $x_i=-a.$
- ${x_i^2}=0$ gives equations of two coincident lines $x_i =0$ and $-x_i=0.$
- $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ is equivalent to $b^2x_1^2+a^2x_2^2=0$ which in turn gives a single point, the origin, since the sum of two squares is $0$ if and only if both squares are $0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7fa5c07c-714f-555e-9253-e8c6b56484e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5130 :tutorial/title "Degenerate (Real) Quadratic Curves"} :step/id #uuid "e4b30b5f-3e46-516c-bdb2-28d2099fba5a" :step/math-academy-id 32210 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172921}} {:db/id 17592186173166 :tutorial/content "There are also a few so-called *degenerate (real) quadratic curves:*

| Standard Equation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ | Pair of<br> intersecting lines |
| ${x_i^2}=a^2$ | Pair of <br> parallel lines |
| ${x_i^2}=0$ | Pair of <br> coincident lines |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ | Single point |

Let's see why these equations define the described curves:

- $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ is equivalent to $(bx_1 - ax_2)(bx_1 + ax_2)=0$ which in turn gives equations of two lines $bx_1 - ax_2=0$ and $bx_1 + ax_2=0$ intersecting at the origin.
- ${x_i^2}=a^2$ is equivalent to $(x_i - a)(x_i + a)=0$ which in turn gives equations of two parallel lines $x_i =a$ and $x_i=-a.$
- ${x_i^2}=0$ gives equations of two coincident lines $x_i =0$ and $-x_i=0.$
- $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=0$ is equivalent to $b^2x_1^2+a^2x_2^2=0$ which in turn gives a single point, the origin, since the sum of two squares is $0$ if and only if both squares are $0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7fa5c07c-714f-555e-9253-e8c6b56484e7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5130 :tutorial/title "Degenerate (Real) Quadratic Curves"} {:db/id 17592186172921 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173167 :tutorial/content "Finally, some quadratic equations might define an *empty set* (or so-called *imaginary curve*):

| Standard Equation | Description |
| --- | --- |
| $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2}=-1$ | Imaginary ellipse |
| $x_i^2=-a^2$ | Pair of imaginary<br> parallel lines |

Let's see why these equations define the described curves:

- Although there are no real solutions, the equation $\dfrac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{b^2} = -1,$ which is equivalent to $\dfrac{x_1^2}{(a\textrm{i})^2} + \dfrac{x_2^2}{(b\textrm{i})^2} = 1,$ has imaginary solutions, so we could interpret this as an imaginary ellipse.
- Although there are no real solutions, the equation ${x_i^2}=-a^2$ is equivalent to $(x_i - a\textrm{i})(x_i + a\textrm{i})=0$ which in turn gives equations of two imaginary parallel lines $x_i =a\textrm{i}$ and $x_i=-a\textrm{i}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "81eb37e3-202d-5934-93ce-8534c3ffc1a0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5131 :tutorial/title "Empty Sets"} :step/id #uuid "980cb0f2-0635-5e7b-926e-f8cbd302bf7b" :step/math-academy-id 32211 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172888}} {:db/id 17592186173167 :tutorial/content "Finally, some quadratic equations might define an *empty set* (or so-called *imaginary curve*):

:topic/math-academy-id 1275} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106917 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107063 :tutorial/content "The formula for the area of a general triangle is

$$
\mathcal{A}=\frac{1}{2}{\color{red}{a}}{\color{blue}{b}}\sin{C},
$$

where $\color{red}a$ and $\color{blue}b$ are two sides of the triangle and $C$ is the measure of the angle between those sides (called the **included angle**).

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

To demonstrate how this works, suppose that we want to calculate the area of the non-right-angled triangle below:

![](images/4b/4b0fb75f9b2eaf3d0237d8cfe2e31bc27b02425b6cffa8d15f27d6de03f60838.png)

Let's call the lengths of the sides $BC = \color{red}{a}$ and $AC ={\color{blue}{b}}.$ For the triangle above we have
${\color{red}a=10},$ ${\color{blue}b=12},$ and  $m\angle C=45^{\circ}.$

Therefore, the area of our triangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10\cdot 12\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\  & =60\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =30\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ff9f9791-f688-59c5-8c9d-b776016045be" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2465 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e26490ba-2418-5a78-9c31-5425d1b67c42" :step/math-academy-id :step/next {:db/id 17592186106922}} {:db/id 17592186106922 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107027 :tutorial/content "Consider $\triangle ABC$ with sides of lengths $a,b,$ and $c,$ as shown below.

![](images/1d/1d30e12e2252b27a651bb02b718cf2214c7ddcf4f0e768c5bd952c11b2e4ecde.png)

Let's now add the height of length $h$ perpendicular to $\overline{BC},$ as shown.

![](images/96/96817ab2168b9ec37777166a26001ee8bc7e7709f80fdf234ac6d70cdfbb5ddc.png)

Using the usual formula for the area $\mathcal A$ of a triangle in terms of its base and height, we have

$$
\mathcal A = \dfrac12 ah.
$$

Using elementary trigonometry, we have that

$$
\dfrac{h}{b} = \sin C
$$

which means that 

$$
h = b\sin C.
$$

Therefore, by substituting this into our expression for $\mathcal A,$ we have

$$
\mathcal A = \dfrac12ab\sin C
$$

as required.

We can use a similar approach to prove the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ A & =\frac{1}{2}ac\operatorname{sin}⁡B\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e126d83f-0c01-514b-bb7e-ce2d16291b22" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13277 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Area of a General Triangle"} :step/id #uuid "29c5a503-b01d-5845-a29d-0bd76807b33f" :step/math-academy-id 655408}] :activity/title "The Area of a General Triangle" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105954} {:db/id 17592186106917 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107063 :tutorial/content "The formula for the area of a general triangle is

$$
\mathcal{A}=\frac{1}{2}{\color{red}{a}}{\color{blue}{b}}\sin{C},
$$

where $\color{red}a$ and $\color{blue}b$ are two sides of the triangle and $C$ is the measure of the angle between those sides (called the **included angle**).

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

To demonstrate how this works, suppose that we want to calculate the area of the non-right-angled triangle below:

![](images/4b/4b0fb75f9b2eaf3d0237d8cfe2e31bc27b02425b6cffa8d15f27d6de03f60838.png)

Let's call the lengths of the sides $BC = \color{red}{a}$ and $AC ={\color{blue}{b}}.$ For the triangle above we have
${\color{red}a=10},$ ${\color{blue}b=12},$ and  $m\angle C=45^{\circ}.$

Therefore, the area of our triangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10\cdot 12\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\  & =60\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =30\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ff9f9791-f688-59c5-8c9d-b776016045be" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2465 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e26490ba-2418-5a78-9c31-5425d1b67c42" :step/math-academy-id 655395 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106918}} {:db/id 17592186107063 :tutorial/content "The formula for the area of a general triangle is

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=3.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})=\frac{1-x}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{1+\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{\sqrt{x}(3-x)}{3}(\frac{x+1}{2\sqrt{x}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3-x)(x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3+2x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {[3x+{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129217 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129036 :question/id #uuid "fcfc9339-efd3-525f-a6f3-695124724e1c" :question/math-academy-id "e-9120"} :knowledge-point/id Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts (see figure above). What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =\pm n\pi ,\,n\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049491} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "81f78a7c-cd88-56d1-8f8c-3b34e686486a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value :step/math-academy-id 33991 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130112}} {:db/id 17592186130114 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130413 :tutorial/content "Consider the arc of the curve $y=f(x)$ that lies between the vertical lines $x=x_1$ and $x=x_2,$ as shown below on the left. By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution,** as shown below on the right. How can we find its surface area?

![](images/d9/d929311a1d86da82fd2acb517ed148715273d37a66928f0cb2949353e06457e1.png)

First, we divide the interval $[a,b]$ into small subintervals, each of length $\Delta{x}.$ Let's consider a part of the curve that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of the corresponding curved arc be $\Delta{s}.$ When this part of the curve is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a closed strip. 

![](images/55/55ff01b354818b7ec3b9240d470acfa14c648b967f142b7554c172d12e2ca57b.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that both left and right radii of the strip are approximately equal to $y=f(x).$ Then, this strip can be viewed as the lateral surface of a right cylinder with height $h=\Delta{s}$ and radius $r=y=f(x).$ 

![](images/5a/5a71ce7729d37ca3d1fb86067f0d3f2233243a24710d08132dfc63f372bb6521.png)

We can approximate the lateral surface area of such a cylinder as

$$
S_{\text{strip}} \approx S_{\text{cylinder}} = 2\pi r \cdot h = 2\pi y \cdot \Delta{s}.
$$

The sum over all subintervals will approximate the total area $S$ that we want. The approximation becomes more and more accurate as $\Delta{s} \to 0$. Therefore, to get the area of the surface, we need to integrate:

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s
$$

Recall that for a curve $y = f(x),$ the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution,** as shown below on the right. How can we find its surface area?

![](images/d9/d929311a1d86da82fd2acb517ed148715273d37a66928f0cb2949353e06457e1.png)

First, we divide the interval $[a,b]$ into small subintervals, each of length $\Delta{x}.$ Let's consider a part of the curve that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of the corresponding curved arc be $\Delta{s}.$ When this part of the curve is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a closed strip. 

![](images/55/55ff01b354818b7ec3b9240d470acfa14c648b967f142b7554c172d12e2ca57b.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that both left and right radii of the strip are approximately equal to $y=f(x).$ Then, this strip can be viewed as the lateral surface of a right cylinder with height $h=\Delta{s}$ and radius $r=y=f(x).$ 

![](images/5a/5a71ce7729d37ca3d1fb86067f0d3f2233243a24710d08132dfc63f372bb6521.png)

We can approximate the lateral surface area of such a cylinder as

$$
S_{\text{strip}} \approx S_{\text{cylinder}} = 2\pi r \cdot h = 2\pi y \cdot \Delta{s}.
$$

The sum over all subintervals will approximate the total area $S$ that we want. The approximation becomes more and more accurate as $\Delta{s} \to 0$. Therefore, to get the area of the surface, we need to integrate:

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s
$$

Recall that for a curve $y = f(x),$ the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we can find the total surface area using the formula

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f7ed0d58-7855-54cd-952c-8f23fe9c6678" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5532 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9fe394ca-d35a-573c-8c77-ab458259c696" :step/math-academy-id 34375 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130111}} {:db/id 17592186130111 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129215 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129034 :question/id #uuid "fdf51620-58e9-5886-93e5-02a814b154bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-8905"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "84167caa-9fa6-5162-a598-c2dd11d9ed85" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049191} {:db/id 17592186050217}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129410} {:db/id 17592186129411} {:db/id 17592186235464} {:db/id 17592186244234} {:db/id 17592186244235} {:db/id 17592186244237} {:db/id 17592186262623} {:db/id 17592186386371} {:db/id 17592186430039} {:db/id 17592186430042}] :knowledge-point/title "Integrals Representing Surface Areas Generated by Functions of X"} :step/id #uuid "dcc3ef91-e52c-5a24-9e81-8b2613846183" :step/math-academy-id 33265 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130115}} {:db/id 17592186130115 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130414 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given a curve of the form $x=f(y)$ that lies between the horizontal lines $y=y_1$ and $y=y_2.$ How do we calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?

What is the unit rate of miles per gallon of gas?" :question/worked-solution "To compute the unit rate of miles per gallon of gas, we divide the number of miles, $15$, by the number of gallons of gas,

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

as follows:

$$
15 \div \dfrac{3}{4}
$$

To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the fraction's reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
15 \div \frac{3}{4} &= 15 \cdot \frac{4}{3} \\
&= \frac{15}{1} \cdot \frac{4}{3} \\
&= \frac{15 \cdot 4}{1 \cdot 3} \\
&= \frac{60}{3} \\
&= 20
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit rate is $20$ miles per gallon of gas."} {:db/id 17592186049357} {:db/id 17592186050195} {:db/id 17592186152646 :question/id #uuid "3d1cba23-ee84-559a-950a-b7d528c5c6c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-67813" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186152104 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2e3e8809-2164-543d-bb0a-c6a20cc7de6b" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of an Integer and a Fraction"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8ea38938-101c-5627-b633-5ed8a7a16e24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$48$ feet per second" :db/id 17592186150384} {:answer/id #uuid "b3688ffd-9141-591e-b0a7-5a2afb425c3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$52$ feet per second" :db/id 17592186150385} {:answer/id #uuid "b9ffc2d8-74a2-541b-90c6-32b27b02168d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$46$ feet per second" :db/id 17592186150386} {:answer/id #uuid "c7515aae-c4ad-5d67-9431-e0caf81d5091" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$42$ feet per second" :db/id 17592186150387} {:answer/id #uuid "42f32271-86ab-5546-9fe1-7079e8fbd060" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$44$ feet per second" :db/id 17592186150388}] :answer-field/id #uuid "28ad58b4-b6cf-57e3-ac26-291900a23a7b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186150383}] :question/problem "A skydiver falls $40$ feet in $\frac{5}{6}$ seconds. How many tablespoons is $1$ gram of olive oil?" :question/worked-solution "To find the number of tablespoons in $1$ gram of olive oil, we can compute the unit rate of tablespoons per gram olive oil. We do this by dividing the number of tablespoons,

$$
\dfrac{1}{3}
$$

by the number of grams, $4$, as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{3} \div 4
$$

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{3} \div 4 &= \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\
&= \frac{1 \cdot 1}{3 \cdot 4} \\
&= \frac{1}{12}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is

$$
\dfrac{1}{12}

How many miles can Martha swim in $1$ hour?" :question/worked-solution "To find the number of miles that Martha can swim in $1$ hour, we can compute the unit rate of miles per hour. We do this by dividing the number of miles,

$$
\dfrac{3}{4}
$$

by the number of hours,

$$
\dfrac{2}{3}
$$

as follows:

$$
\dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

Dividing a fraction by another fraction is equivalent to multiplying the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{2}{3} &= \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{3}{2} \\
&= \frac{3 \cdot 3}{4 \cdot 2} \\
&= \frac{9}{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the resulting improper fraction as a mixed number:

$$
\dfrac{9}{8} = 1 \, \textrm{R} 1 = 1 \, \dfrac{1}{8}
$$

Therefore, Martha can swim

$$
1 \, \dfrac{1}{8}
$$

miles in $1$ hour."} {:db/id 17592186049616} {:db/id 17592186152650 :question/id #uuid "1e1f7bde-6465-5da4-b505-7301d0c0729e" :question/math-academy-id "q-67826"} {:db/id 17592186152651 :question/id #uuid "2761f039-d13a-562d-9bd0-6270f04a74fe" :question/math-academy-id "q-67829" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186152106 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "87385cd2-8143-54de-9995-e1cc2ecf06c0" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of a Fraction and a Fraction"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8d72f22d-7c27-57e3-a44b-1437dcf4f194" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186150414} {:answer/id #uuid "a9dc4aad-6d45-5655-8956-808d040c790f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186150415} {:answer/id #uuid "cf3be800-234b-5411-9dcc-798fd26de0f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3\frac{3}{6}" :db/id 17592186150416} {:answer/id #uuid "d5747382-778d-5aef-bc47-1305a53de870" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186150417} {:answer/id #uuid "fed1b810-85ef-5011-b00f-2930e8117be4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186150418}] :answer-field/id #uuid "284d2c18-88a4-50e8-a2d2-75fa19b0e1f7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186150413}] :question/problem "Jim ran $\frac{5}{6}$ of a mile in $\frac{1}{5}$ of an hour. 17592186153341 :tutorial/content "A **unit rate** is a ratio of two quantities stated as some amount of one quantity per unit of the other quantity.

For example, suppose that Carl can run $100$ meters in $20$ seconds. The unit rate is how many meters Carl can run in $1$ second. To compute Carl's unit rate, we divide the number of meters by the number of seconds:

$$
100 \div 20 = 5
$$

So, the unit rate is $5$ meters per second. In other words, Carl can run $5$ meters in $1$ second.

Unit rates do not always come out to whole numbers. For example, suppose Jamie can run $100$ meters in $15$ seconds. To compute Jamie's unit rate, we again divide the number of meters by the number of seconds:

$$
\begin{aligned}
100 \div 15 &= \frac{100}{15} \\
&= \frac{100 \div 5}{15 \div 5} \\
&= \frac{20}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the resulting improper fraction as a mixed number, we get

$$
\dfrac{20}{3} = 6 \, \textrm{R} 2 = 6 \, \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

Therefore, Jamie can run

$$
6 \, \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

meters per second." :tutorial/id #uuid "9f08d42f-43a3-595e-92b3-d634f656ce2e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3073 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "33197a11-fb17-59b2-b2dc-f9c9927714b9" :step/math-academy-id 16684 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152976}}] :activity/title "Unit Rates Associated With Ratios of Fractions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152308} {:db/id 17592186152988 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153341 :tutorial/content "A **unit rate** is a ratio of two quantities stated as some amount of one quantity per unit of the other quantity.

exponential decay expression or function.

For example, suppose that, due to overfishing, a fish population decays exponentially. The population $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = 5\,000 \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^t,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began. What can we deduce about the population of fish from this model?

The first thing to notice is that the function above is an exponential decay function of the form

$$
y(t) = a \cdot b^t.
$$

So, we can deduce the following:

- $a=5\,000$ represents the initial value. So this tells us that there were $5\,000$ fish when the overfishing began.

- $b = \dfrac 1 2$ is the decay factor. Since $0 < b < 1,$ this tells us that we're dealing with exponential decay, *not* exponential growth (for exponential growth we need $b > 1$).

- $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began." :tutorial/id #uuid "adec391e-8573-55bf-b53b-d5d15177f633" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1970 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid - $a=5\,000$ represents the initial value. So this tells us that there were $5\,000$ fish when the overfishing began.

- $b = \dfrac 1 2$ is the decay factor. Since $0 < b < 1,$ this tells us that we're dealing with exponential decay, *not* exponential growth (for exponential growth we need $b > 1$).

- $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began." :tutorial/id #uuid "adec391e-8573-55bf-b53b-d5d15177f633" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1970 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b36f7829-7634-567d-9517-b3c22769bd8e" :step/math-academy-id 7129 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116359}} {:db/id 17592186116434 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to interpret various aspects of an exponential decay expression or function.

For example, suppose that, due to overfishing, a fish population decays exponentially. The population $y(t)$ is given by

$$
y(t) = 5\,000 \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^t,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began. What can we deduce about the population of fish from this model?

The first thing to notice is that the function above is an exponential decay function of the form

$$
y(t) = a \cdot b^t.
$$

So, we can deduce the following:

- $a=5\,000$ represents the initial value. So this tells us that there were $5\,000$ fish when the overfishing began.

- $b = \dfrac 1 2$ is the decay factor. Since $0 < b < 1,$ this tells us that we're dealing with exponential decay, *not* exponential growth (for exponential growth we need $b > 1$).

- $t$ is the time, in months, since the overfishing began." :tutorial/id #uuid "adec391e-8573-55bf-b53b-d5d15177f633" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1970 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186158355 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158438 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to *find the roots* of a function using *Newton’s method*. That is, we solved equations of the form

$$
f(x) = 0,
$$

by starting with an initial guess and refining it step by step using the update rule

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
$$

Now, we turn to a closely related problem of *finding a local minimum or maximum* of a function $f(x)$. Recall that these may occur at points where the derivative $f'(x)$ is equal to zero. In other words, we are looking for the roots of the function's derivative.

Earlier, we approximated the function by a straight line near our current guess. Here, instead of using a linear approximation, we assume that the function $f(x)$ behaves like a *parabola* near our current guess. That’s a reasonable assumption if $f$ is smooth. 

To make this idea precise, we use a second-order Taylor approximation, $F(x){:}$

$$
F(x) = f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(x - x_n) + \dfrac{1}{2} f''(x_n)(x - x_n)^2
$$

To find the minimum or maximum, we first need to take the derivative of this approximation, which is

$$
F'(x) = f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n).
$$

We then need to set $F'(x) =0$:

$$
f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n) = 0
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$  as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}({x}_{n})(x-{x}_{n}) & =-{f}^{′}({x}_{n}) \\ x-{x}_{n} & =-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})} \\ x & ={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})}\end{aligned}
$$

So, just like in root-finding, we start with an initial guess and improve it step by step. But this time, we apply Newton’s method to the derivative $f'(x)$ instead of the function $f(x)$ itself:

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)}
$$

**Note**: The second derivative $f''(x_n)$ must not be zero. If it is zero, or even very close to zero, the update step can become extremely large, leading us far away from the solution.

Just like in root-finding, Newton’s method works best when the function is smooth, and our initial guess is already close to the minimum or maximum." :tutorial/id #uuid "0745939b-5be0-5c57-bc01-4f0f87024707" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10738 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ba6dbaa2-2df5-5b25-ad1e-3045a5009cb6" :step/math-academy-id 688822 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158356}} {:db/id 17592186158356 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158457 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function 

$$
f(x)= \ln(x+1)+\dfrac{2}{x+1}
$$

in the interval $[0,2].$ Let's calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting at the point $x_0=0.8.$ 

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)},
$$

where $f'(x_n)$ and $f''(x_n)$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n,$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{2}{x+1})}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{4}{(x+1)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3-x}{(x+1)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{\frac{{x}_{n}-1}{({x}_{n}+1)^{2}}}{\frac{3-{x}_{n}}{({x}_{n}+1)^{3}}} \\  & ={x}_{n}-\frac{{x}_{n}^{2}-1}{3-{x}_{n}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with $x_0=0.8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-\frac{{x}_{0}^{2}-1}{3-{x}_{0}} \\  & =0.8-\frac{(0.8)^{2}-1}{3-0.8} \\  & ≈0.964,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "8b8920e9-7fa3-56ff-ab8e-2d0283bc3911" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13141 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157519} {:db/id 17592186158355 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158438 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to *find the roots* of a function using *Newton’s method*. That is, we solved equations of the form

$$
f(x) = 0,
$$

by starting with an initial guess and refining it step by step using the update rule

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
$$

Now, we turn to a closely related problem of *finding a local minimum or maximum* of a function $f(x)$. Recall that these may occur at points where the derivative $f'(x)$ is equal to zero. In other words, we are looking for the roots of the function's derivative.

Earlier, we approximated the function by a straight line near our current guess. Here, instead of using a linear approximation, we assume that the function $f(x)$ behaves like a *parabola* near our current guess. That’s a reasonable assumption if $f$ is smooth. 

To make this idea precise, we use a second-order Taylor approximation, $F(x){:}$

$$
F(x) = f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(x - x_n) + \dfrac{1}{2} f''(x_n)(x - x_n)^2
$$

To find the minimum or maximum, we first need to take the derivative of this approximation, which is

$$
F'(x) = f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n).
$$

We then need to set $F'(x) =0$:

$$
f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n) = 0
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$  as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}({x}_{n})(x-{x}_{n}) & =-{f}^{′}({x}_{n}) \\ x-{x}_{n} & =-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})} \\ x & ={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})}\end{aligned}
$$

So, just like in root-finding, we start with an initial guess and improve it step by step. But this time, we apply Newton’s method to the derivative $f'(x)$ instead of the function $f(x)$ itself:

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)}
$$

**Note**: The second derivative $f''(x_n)$ must not be zero. If it is zero, or even very close to zero, the update step can become extremely large, leading us far away from the solution.

Just like in root-finding, Newton’s method works best when the function is smooth, and our initial guess is already close to the minimum or maximum." :tutorial/id #uuid "0745939b-5be0-5c57-bc01-4f0f87024707" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10738 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ba6dbaa2-2df5-5b25-ad1e-3045a5009cb6" :step/math-academy-id 688822 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158356}} {:db/id 17592186158438 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to *find the roots* of a function using *Newton’s method*. $$
f(x)= \ln(x+1)+\dfrac{2}{x+1}
$$

in the interval $[0,2].$ Let's calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting at the point $x_0=0.8.$ 

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)},
$$

where $f'(x_n)$ and $f''(x_n)$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n,$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{2}{x+1})}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{4}{(x+1)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3-x}{(x+1)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{\frac{{x}_{n}-1}{({x}_{n}+1)^{2}}}{\frac{3-{x}_{n}}{({x}_{n}+1)^{3}}} \\  & ={x}_{n}-\frac{{x}_{n}^{2}-1}{3-{x}_{n}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with $x_0=0.8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-\frac{{x}_{0}^{2}-1}{3-{x}_{0}} \\  & =0.8-\frac{(0.8)^{2}-1}{3-0.8} \\  & ≈0.964,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "8b8920e9-7fa3-56ff-ab8e-2d0283bc3911" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13141 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "b9795715-d19d-577f-99a4-49bef78578e8" :step/math-academy-id 688823 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158357}} {:db/id 17592186158457 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function
