17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t).
$$

Given that the solution to the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-t}+\begin{bmatrix}b \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution of the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-1-(-1) & 0 \\ 3 & -1-(-1)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0 \\ 3{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-t}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, we see that $a=0,b=\frac{1}{3},$ and $a+b=\frac{1}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186399138 :question/id #uuid "8179a1bc-9dd2-5c9c-a7dd-3de3a7cd250c" :question/math-academy-id "q-80917" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186157446 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c19f9d9-fa4b-5261-b9a0-99a203aeac30" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the General Solution to a System of Linear Equations in a Defective Case"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66613f28-b688-5af5-87c4-a12f46f9bd0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186399140} {:answer/id #uuid "b467a51e-f9be-5bed-89bc-7ff012c894de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186399141} {:answer/id #uuid "149698b5-3361-5f52-a32c-6ed656acfe8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186399142} {:answer/id #uuid "748a5bc0-46b6-5698-846f-66d6952f985d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186399143} {:answer/id #uuid "99a4d6e3-caf9-544f-ba67-8f950954be82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186399144}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "66613f28-b688-5af5-87c4-a12f46f9bd0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186399140} :answer-field/id #uuid "d2967834-56c7-54af-a045-1eb688f37565" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186399139}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the system of linear differential equations given by

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =5$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}\,),

$$

$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+2{w}_{2} &=1 \\ 0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$ we get 

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{5t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}{e}^{5t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

$$

$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-3-(-3) & -6 \\ 0 & -3-(-3)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}-6{w}_{2} &=1 \\ 0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{2}=-\frac{1}{6}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{1}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{1}=0,$  we get

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{6}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -\frac{1}{6}\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ -\frac{{c}_{2}}{6}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ -\frac{{c}_{2}}{6}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}-12 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-3t}+\begin{bmatrix}-12 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-3t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}(1-12t){e}^{-3t} \\ 2\,{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186302268 :question/id #uuid "26bb41ab-79e8-5c9f-95c2-ae20713f031a" :question/math-academy-id "q-326239"} {:db/id 17592186348421 :question/id #uuid :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186351124}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t),\,x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}.$

Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the repeated eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (of multiplicity two).
For this eigenvalue, we get 

$$
A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}∼\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
$v=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda $ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $v$, the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}v{e}^{\lambda t}+{c}_{2}(vt{e}^{\lambda t}+w{e}^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

To find $w,$ we solve the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2+2 & 0 \\ 5 & -2+2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=0 \\ 5{w}_{1}+0{w}_{2} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

So, we obtain

$$
{w}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

The variable ${w}_{2}$ is a free variable. Setting ${w}_{2}=0,$  we get

$$
w=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-2t}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}),\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Now, we need to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial condition $x(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$ Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{c}_{2}}{5} \\ {c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{c}_{2}}{5} \\ {c}_{1}\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-2t}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}. \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-2t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} \\ (2+5t){e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186394078 :question/id #uuid "6e25df6c-8786-547c-9562-9085a352e6d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-80928"} {:db/id 17592186394092 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186158391 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158467 :tutorial/content "For a $2 \times 2$ system of linear differential equations

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),
$$

 
we know that if $A$ is diagonalizable and has eigenvectors ${\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues ${\color{black}\lambda_1}$ and ${\color{black}\lambda_2},$ respectively, then the general solution formula is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

But what happens if $A$ has a single repeated eigenvalue, $\lambda?$ It depends on the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda.$

- We say that $\lambda$ is a **complete** eigenvalue if there are two linearly independent eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to $\lambda.$

- We say that $\lambda$ is a **defective** (or **incomplete**) eigenvalue if there is only one linearly independent eigenvector $\mathbf v$ corresponding to $\lambda.$

This leads to two distinct cases:

- *The Complete Case.* If $\lambda$ is a *complete* eigenvalue, then there are two linearly independent eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to $\lambda,$ and we can use the usual formula:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda} t}
$$

- *The Defective Case.* If $\lambda$ is a *defective* eigenvalue, there is only one linearly independent eigenvector $\mathbf v.$ We cannot use the usual formula because there are not enough eigenvectors.

Instead, we must find a *generalized eigenvector* $\mathbf w,$ which is a vector that satisfies the equation

$$
(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.
$$

The general solution is then given by the formula: 

$$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

But what happens if $A$ has a single repeated eigenvalue, $\lambda?$ It depends on the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda.$

- We say that $\lambda$ is a **complete** eigenvalue if there are two linearly independent eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to $\lambda.$

- We say that $\lambda$ is a **defective** (or **incomplete**) eigenvalue if there is only one linearly independent eigenvector $\mathbf v$ corresponding to $\lambda.$

- *The Complete Case.* If $\lambda$ is a *complete* eigenvalue, then there are two linearly independent eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ corresponding to $\lambda,$ and we can use the usual formula:

$$

Instead, we must find a *generalized eigenvector* $\mathbf w,$ which is a vector that satisfies the equation

$$

The general solution is then given by the formula: 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}  + c_2 (\mathbf{v}  te^{\lambda t}  +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, )
$$

We'll explain how and why this solution comes about at the end of the lesson.

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

{{field-2}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3xy &=0 \\ -5y+4xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3xy & =0 \\ x(2-3y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{3}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{3},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4xy & =0 \\ y(-5+4x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(-5+4x) & =0 \\ -5+4x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186167256 :question/id #uuid "f0f816f5-6732-572e-beb4-ba284ca82c1b" :question/math-academy-id "q-334992"} {:db/id 17592186370181 :question/id #uuid "4ef04316-d6de-5c0d-a680-25266abf9b77" :question/math-academy-id "q-334998" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f7ca91be-1147-5049-8064-d763eb6133e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186370183}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370183} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f4acca5-dac1-54fa-9e21-9915bff82215" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370182} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "412cc220-b5ee-5f02-87a4-33b233723962" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/id 17592186370185}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370185} :answer-field/id #uuid "96278b61-4187-511e-8e54-0a1a2d062155" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370184}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-2xy)=4-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+5xy)=5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+5xy)=-3+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}4-2y & -2x \\ 5y & -3+5x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}4-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 5(0) & -3+5(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$"} {{field-6}}{{field-7}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-0.5x+0.5xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=y-5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=-0.5+0.5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=0.5x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-5xy)=1-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5y & 0.5x \\ -5y & 1-5x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5(1) & 0.5(0.2) \\ -5(1) & 1-5(0.2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.1 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-5)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.5\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source)."} :topic/math-academy-id 3191} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167867 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168012 :tutorial/content "The **Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model** describes the interaction between two species (predator and prey) and is given by the nonlinear system of the form

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants. Here, 

- $x=x(t)$ is the *prey population*, and

- $y=y(t)$ is the *predator population*.

Remember that a derivative represents a *rate of change*.

- In the first equation, $x' = ax - bxy,$ the prey changes due to the following:

- The *intrinsic growth*, which is given by the $ax$ term. If there are no predators ($y=0$), then $x' = ax > 0$ and the prey grows exponentially.

- The *predation*, which is given by the $-bxy$ term. When prey and predators interact, the term $-bxy$ decreases $x.$

- In the second equation, $y' = -cy + dxy,$ the predators change due to the following:

- The *intrinsic decay*, which is given by the $-cy$ term. If there is no prey ($x=0$), then $y' = -cy < 0$ and predators decline exponentially.

- The *feeding/reproduction*, which is given by the $dxy$ term. When prey and predators interact, the term $dxy$ increases $y.$

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "df04c110-07af-507a-9a45-8cef3122f2d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14531 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ca5cf22c-180f-58ff-8262-fb95f4fb6109" :step/math-academy-id 589726 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167868}} {:db/id 17592186167868 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166922 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166557 :question/id #uuid "2266e14f-c662-5844-bfb4-3b4259f9232a" :question/math-academy-id "e-21734"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "16481b80-9744-5c8d-843a-14af30fd8cf4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048835}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167249} {:db/id 17592186167250} {:db/id 17592186370156} {:db/id 17592186370163} {:db/id 17592186370170} {:db/id 17592186391519} {:db/id 17592186396536} {:db/id 17592186445106} {:db/id 17592186445109} {:db/id 17592186445110}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying and Interpreting the Lotka-Volterra Model"} :step/id #uuid "a7a45fab-41bd-5b22-9d1d-e4566baed3a5" :step/math-academy-id 589727 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167874}} {:db/id 17592186167869 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166923 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166554 :question/id #uuid "037b7db9-131c-5a08-aa84-d7552a903e11" :question/math-academy-id "e-21726"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4f77fc78-6c6b-5dd0-ac2b-7822e4cb961f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167245} {:db/id 17592186167256} {:db/id 17592186370181} {:db/id 17592186370186} {:db/id 17592186370191} {:db/id 17592186370196} {:db/id 17592186445105} {:db/id 17592186445111}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Equilibrium Points of the Lotka-Volterra System"} :step/id #uuid "c0b5125d-8295-5d89-bd4b-316c26197a12" :step/math-academy-id 589730 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167870}} {:db/id 17592186167870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168013 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax-bxy)=a-by,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax-bxy)=-bx \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/e1/e1c9a7c83c6c5790b264670bba4c8e7352ac18239b737348a85c393b5de3be6e.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/7a/7a3543ed5d9733302a80e87b344d4f74d46d9bc27d5a034692b81cec54a56635.svg) to get

![](images/24/24ac6a3fb192074570c1bf62585a5b8e57e6052b6118159c8f1645a31d92b21f.svg)

Since this matrix is diagonal, the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries: $\lambda_1 = a$ and $\lambda_2 = -c.$ Because $a,c$ are positive constants, we have $\lambda_1 > 0$ and $\lambda_2 < 0.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*." :tutorial/id #uuid "36f1f197-5258-587f-b119-95ff77bb685a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14532 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "41a5a760-4fcc-5875-91b1-93493893b0f7" :step/math-academy-id 589733 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167875}} {:db/id 17592186167871 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166924 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166555 :question/id #uuid "47c1e08d-d5b4-5f1e-b225-d1336645898f" :question/math-academy-id "e-21727"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f1fa1647-1acb-50bd-95e7-26ed0c495bd4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048881}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167246} {:db/id 17592186167247} {:db/id 17592186370201} {:db/id 17592186370240} {:db/id 17592186445104} {:db/id 17592186445107} {:db/id 17592186514444}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model"} :step/id #uuid "6b342954-1db0-5d02-a6a8-84bfa7a0897d" :step/math-academy-id 589734 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167872}} {:db/id 17592186167872 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168014 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider a typical curved trajectory in more detail.

![](images/73/7330af149428dd84fa1e94fd914a1e71d074f38bfe4ced44928a3c7043ee4fe9.png)

It can be split into four parts by the lines $x=\dfrac{c}{d}$ and $y=\dfrac{a}{b}$ passing through the nonzero equilibrium:

- From $A$ to $B,$ the number of prey *decreases* and the number of predators *increases*.

- From $B$ to $C,$ the number of prey *decreases* and the number of predators *decreases*.

- From $C$ to $D,$ the number of prey *increases* and the number of predators *decreases*.

- From $D$ to $A,$ the number of prey *increases* and the number of predators *increases*.

The corresponding population dynamics graphs look as depicted below.

![](images/1d/1d04db41fdc9fd8940dec3a130c4dc2a26bd4b3fa3861f40f65b0c708cb16084.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "310e1e78-8811-5cee-b6ef-0c42f8ff1481" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14533 :tutorial/title "Population Dynamics Graph"} :step/id #uuid "75643098-713e-56c0-9776-9d37e4b4c88a" :step/math-academy-id 589737 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167873}} {:db/id 17592186167873 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166925 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166556 :question/id #uuid "98a0cd06-80a8-514c-bc89-c739d8502fda" :question/math-academy-id "e-21728"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c9c2220-030e-5418-915c-e34d7962c077" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167248} {:db/id 17592186167257} {:db/id 17592186370279} {:db/id 17592186370293} {:db/id 17592186370369} {:db/id 17592186445108}] :knowledge-point/title "Analyzing a Solution of the Lotka-Volterra Model Given the Phase Portrait"} :step/id #uuid "7accc131-3365-5964-b248-f0c1fe8fe597" :step/math-academy-id 589738} {:db/id 17592186167874 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168026 :tutorial/content "Recall that the equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $\mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, for the Lotka–Volterra model 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}ax-bxy &=0 \\ -cy+dxy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ax-bxy & =0 \\ x(a-by) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\dfrac{a}{b}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+d(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\dfrac{a}{b},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0 \\ \frac{a}{b}(-c+dx) & =0 \\ -c+dx & =0 \\ x & =\frac{c}{d}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d},\dfrac{a}{b}\right).$

Therefore, there are two equilibria:

- The *origin* $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{(0,0)}.$

- The *nonzero equilibrium* $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\left(\dfrac{c}{d},\,\dfrac{a}{b}\right)}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c4f47199-6618-59ac-aa11-c5d0bc8ff50f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14592 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} :step/id #uuid "9636d5a8-52d6-57c2-8a64-64ff786d40da" :step/math-academy-id 589752 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167869}} {:db/id 17592186167875 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168027 :tutorial/content "Next, we evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](images/d5/d57e5d0566616dcf983c8d2d9ee8375cb70aa44d4d5933026266396202248d22.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/b3/b3e4462dae63d3e4cbaddcd890e1553dd26372c2fdca8efe87cbfb8984b9a492.svg) to get

![](images/ec/ecc7fb063630624a8acc4ab201208c2cfb86fe97b910cdc6e17fb71629299385.svg)

To find the eigenvalues, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & -\frac{bc}{d} \\ \frac{ad}{b} & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )\cdot (-\lambda )-(-\frac{bc}{d})\cdot \frac{ad}{b} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+ac & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_{1,2} = \pm \sqrt{ac}\,\text{i}.
$$

Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is a *stable center*.

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model, it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues.
However, we will not go into detail on why in this lesson.

Just keep in mind that for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone would be inconclusive in this case (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

Therefore, a typical phase portrait of the system looks as shown below.

![](images/23/236a29ae07d8fd091fd602ad124af53b49754419b949bd42713078bc9d8814b6.png)

The global picture in the first quadrant is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions which intersect at the saddle point $(0,0){:}$

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach infinity (unstable line). Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey increases exponentially.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin (stable line). Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories circle around the nonzero equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d},\dfrac{a}{b}\right).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "73373dc9-48c3-5ba7-b785-32651f0f7563" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14593 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Nonzero Equilibrium"} :step/id #uuid "fce4e25e-7cdb-503e-b918-2448bb55d8cc" :step/math-academy-id 589781 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167871}}] :activity/title "The Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Model" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166989} {:db/id 17592186167867 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168012 :tutorial/content "The **Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model** describes the interaction between two species (predator and prey) and is given by the nonlinear system of the form

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

the equilibria are the solutions of the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}ax-bxy &=0 \\ -cy+dxy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ax-bxy & =0 \\ x(a-by) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\dfrac{a}{b}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+d(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\dfrac{a}{b},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-cy+dxy & =0 \\ y(-c+dx) & =0 \\ \frac{a}{b}(-c+dx) & =0 \\ -c+dx & =0 \\ x & =\frac{c}{d}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{c}{d},\dfrac{a}{b}\right).$

Therefore, there are two equilibria:

- The *origin* $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{(0,0)}.$

- The *nonzero equilibrium* $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\left(\dfrac{c}{d},\,\dfrac{a}{b}\right)}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c4f47199-6618-59ac-aa11-c5d0bc8ff50f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14592 :tutorial/title "Equilibrium Points"} :step/id #uuid "9636d5a8-52d6-57c2-8a64-64ff786d40da" :step/math-academy-id 589752 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167869}} {:db/id 17592186167869 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166923 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166554 :question/id #uuid "037b7db9-131c-5a08-aa84-d7552a903e11" :question/math-academy-id "e-21726"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4f77fc78-6c6b-5dd0-ac2b-7822e4cb961f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167245} {:db/id 17592186167256} {:db/id 17592186370181} {:db/id 17592186370186} {:db/id 17592186370191} {:db/id 17592186370196} {:db/id 17592186445105} {:db/id 17592186445111}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Equilibrium Points of the Lotka-Volterra System"} :step/id #uuid "c0b5125d-8295-5d89-bd4b-316c26197a12" :step/math-academy-id 589730 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167870}} {:db/id 17592186167870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168013 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax-bxy)=a-by,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax-bxy)=-bx \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/e1/e1c9a7c83c6c5790b264670bba4c8e7352ac18239b737348a85c393b5de3be6e.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/7a/7a3543ed5d9733302a80e87b344d4f74d46d9bc27d5a034692b81cec54a56635.svg) to get

![](images/24/24ac6a3fb192074570c1bf62585a5b8e57e6052b6118159c8f1645a31d92b21f.svg)

Since this matrix is diagonal, the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries: $\lambda_1 = a$ and $\lambda_2 = -c.$ Because $a,c$ are positive constants, we have $\lambda_1 > 0$ and $\lambda_2 < 0.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*." :tutorial/id #uuid "36f1f197-5258-587f-b119-95ff77bb685a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14532 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} :step/id #uuid "41a5a760-4fcc-5875-91b1-93493893b0f7" :step/math-academy-id 589733 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167875}} {:db/id 17592186168013 :tutorial/content "Consider the Lotka–Volterra predator-prey model 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′} &=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants, $x=x(t)$ is the prey population, and $y=y(t)$ is the predator population.

To classify the equilibrium at the origin, we need to find the corresponding Jacobian matrix.

Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=ax-bxy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-cy+dxy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(ax-bxy)=a-by,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(ax-bxy)=-bx \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-cy+dxy)=dy,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-cy+dxy)=-c+dx\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](images/e1/e1c9a7c83c6c5790b264670bba4c8e7352ac18239b737348a85c393b5de3be6e.svg)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](images/7a/7a3543ed5d9733302a80e87b344d4f74d46d9bc27d5a034692b81cec54a56635.svg) to get

![](images/24/24ac6a3fb192074570c1bf62585a5b8e57e6052b6118159c8f1645a31d92b21f.svg)

Since this matrix is diagonal, the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries: $\lambda_1 = a$ and $\lambda_2 = -c.$ Because $a,c$ are positive constants, we have $\lambda_1 > 0$ and $\lambda_2 < 0.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an *unstable saddle*." :tutorial/id #uuid "36f1f197-5258-587f-b119-95ff77bb685a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14532 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Origin"} {:db/id 17592186167875 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168027 :tutorial/content "Next, we evaluate the Jacobian matrix
![](images/d5/d57e5d0566616dcf983c8d2d9ee8375cb70aa44d4d5933026266396202248d22.svg)
at the nonzero equilibrium ![](images/b3/b3e4462dae63d3e4cbaddcd890e1553dd26372c2fdca8efe87cbfb8984b9a492.svg) to get

![](images/ec/ecc7fb063630624a8acc4ab201208c2cfb86fe97b910cdc6e17fb71629299385.svg)

To find the eigenvalues, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & -\frac{bc}{d} \\ \frac{ad}{b} & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )\cdot (-\lambda )-(-\frac{bc}{d})\cdot \frac{ad}{b} & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+ac & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_{1,2} = \pm \sqrt{ac}\,\text{i}.
$$

Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is a *stable center*.

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model, it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues.
However, we will not go into detail on why in this lesson.

Just keep in mind that for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone would be inconclusive in this case (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

Therefore, a typical phase portrait of the system looks as shown below.

![](images/23/236a29ae07d8fd091fd602ad124af53b49754419b949bd42713078bc9d8814b6.png)

The global picture in the first quadrant is the following:

- There are two straight-line types of solutions which intersect at the saddle point $(0,0){:}$

- Along the $x$-axis, trajectories approach infinity (unstable line). Indeed, in the absence of the predators, the prey increases exponentially.

- Along the $y$-axis, trajectories approach the origin (stable line). Indeed, in the absence of the prey, the predators decrease exponentially.

- The curved trajectories circle around the nonzero equilibrium point $\left(\dfrac{c}{d},\dfrac{a}{b}\right).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "73373dc9-48c3-5ba7-b785-32651f0f7563" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14593 :tutorial/title "Local Behavior Near the Nonzero Equilibrium"} :step/id #uuid "fce4e25e-7cdb-503e-b918-2448bb55d8cc" :step/math-academy-id 589781 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167871}} {:db/id 17592186167871 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166924 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166555 :question/id #uuid "47c1e08d-d5b4-5f1e-b225-d1336645898f" :question/math-academy-id "e-21727"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f1fa1647-1acb-50bd-95e7-26ed0c495bd4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048881}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167246} {:db/id 17592186167247} {:db/id 17592186370201} {:db/id 17592186370240} {:db/id 17592186445104} {:db/id 17592186445107} {:db/id 17592186514444}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model"} :step/id #uuid "6b342954-1db0-5d02-a6a8-84bfa7a0897d" :step/math-academy-id 589734 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167872}} {:db/id 17592186167872 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168014 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider a typical curved trajectory in more detail.

{{field-6}}{{field-7}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x-2xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-2xy)=4-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+5xy)=5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+5xy)=-3+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}4-2y & -2x \\ 5y & -3+5x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}4-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 5(0) & -3+5(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

$(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3xy &=0 \\ -5y+4xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3xy & =0 \\ x(2-3y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{3}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{3},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4xy & =0 \\ y(-5+4x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(-5+4x) & =0 \\ -5+4x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$"} :step/id #uuid "b096df3e-830d-5b6c-8579-d38d657cdeef" :step/next {:db/id 17592186496338}} {:db/id 17592186496338 :step/content {:db/id 17592186370181 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f7ca91be-1147-5049-8064-d763eb6133e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186370183}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370183} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f4acca5-dac1-54fa-9e21-9915bff82215" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370182} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "412cc220-b5ee-5f02-87a4-33b233723962" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/id 17592186370185}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370185} :answer-field/id #uuid "96278b61-4187-511e-8e54-0a1a2d062155" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370184}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4ef04316-d6de-5c0d-a680-25266abf9b77" :question/math-academy-id "q-334998" :question/problem "$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-2xy)=4-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+5xy)=5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+5xy)=-3+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=\begin{bmatrix}4-2y & -2x \\ 5y & -3+5x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}4-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 5(0) & -3+5(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$"} {{field-6}}{{field-7}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-0.5x+0.5xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=y-5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=-0.5+0.5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=0.5x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-5xy)=1-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5y & 0.5x \\ -5y & 1-5x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5(1) & 0.5(0.2) \\ -5(1) & 1-5(0.2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.1 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-5)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.5\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source)."} :step/id #uuid "a38583d0-39a0-55f8-a293-360a29886e88"} {:db/id 17592186514532 :step/content {:db/id 17592186370186 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d905c7de-54bb-580c-ac14-3568c1b81457" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186370188}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370188} :answer-field/id #uuid "e0bd7840-6559-5707-b910-f2fb5c72d1d1" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370187} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "69850b23-e61d-5814-b226-9ba564c143f6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{5}" :db/id 17592186370190}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370190} :answer-field/id #uuid "4c7dbd36-88be-5be0-b944-7943dca6b4c1" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186370189}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "340e7604-73de-5dd2-91e0-923f082f78e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-334999" :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

$(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x+3xy &=0 \\ 7y-5xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3xy & =0 \\ x(-2+3y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{3}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-5(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{3},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-5xy & =0 \\ y(7-5x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(7-5x) & =0 \\ 7-5x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{7}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{7}{5},\frac{2}{3}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{7}{5},\frac{2}{3}).$"} :step/id #uuid "cc9846dd-5c6b-5fee-8018-43e9e9a516aa" :step/next {:db/id 17592186514520}} {:db/id 17592186514533 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167248 \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=-0.5x+0.5xy \\ {y}^{′} &=y-5xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.2,\,1]^{T},$ we get

{{field-6}}{{field-7}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=-0.5x+0.5xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=y-5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=-0.5+0.5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.5x+0.5xy)=0.5x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5xy)=-5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-5xy)=1-5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5y & 0.5x \\ -5y & 1-5x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-0.5+0.5(1) & 0.5(0.2) \\ -5(1) & 1-5(0.2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.1 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-5)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.5\sqrt{2}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source)."} "340e7604-73de-5dd2-91e0-923f082f78e3" :question/math-academy-id "q-334999" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} &=-2x+3xy \\ {y}^{′} &=7y-5xy\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

$(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x+3xy &=0 \\ 7y-5xy &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3xy & =0 \\ x(-2+3y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{3}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-5(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{3},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-5xy & =0 \\ y(7-5x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(7-5x) & =0 \\ 7-5x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{7}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{7}{5},\frac{2}{3}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{7}{5},\frac{2}{3}).$"} :step/id #uuid "cc9846dd-5c6b-5fee-8018-43e9e9a516aa" :step/next {:db/id 17592186514520}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid ![](images/16/16cbb1865575a8f1d968a065a3b9a09eb6fa3b998a24029d75713825cd5b7a2a.png)" :question/worked-solution "To obtain the given graph, we can perform the following transformations:

- Take the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.
- Reflect the graph in the $x$-axis to get the graph of $y=-\sqrt{x}$.

The result is the solid blue curve shown below.

![](images/78/78b19415feaf4e648e0d49a7aa3a130db5a57cf23b4aeafbdc34e5a968a3bf0e.png)

- Translate the result to the left by $1$ unit to get the graph of $y=-\sqrt{x+1}$.
- Translate the result up by $2$ units to get the graph of $y=-\sqrt{x+1}+2$.

The result is the solid blue curve shown below.

![](images/4f/4ffbc7f9dd9ec50830a671f4ce688f51f6a7a11663f0c93af567ee8cc9a4a4f4.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is

$$
y = -\sqrt{x+1}+2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186111161 :question/id #uuid "c97fd16d-92c5-5b67-9105-54541dc2b4de" :question/math-academy-id "q-38336"} {:db/id 17592186111162 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186111660 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111894 :tutorial/content "The graph of the square root function

$$
y=\sqrt{x}
$$

is shown below.

![](images/a4/a4d6f457f29cc6a292f23029967dc6fbb0c0f3905a04f34a430fddc8b211b0c3.png)

In this lesson, we will learn how to apply graph transformations to the square root function. Let's start by considering translations." :tutorial/id #uuid "ff943ba5-7959-599a-8f13-e5bdb1bda83a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4775 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2d1bbdf9-422b-5f69-8f59-21d910778f63" :step/math-academy-id 464534 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111661}} {:db/id 17592186111661 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111895 :tutorial/content "We can move the graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{x}
$$

up or down by adding or subtracting a number. For example, to obtain the graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{x}-3
$$

we perform the following transformations:

- Take the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.
- Translate the graph **down** by $3$ units to get the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}-3$.

The result is the solid blue curve shown below.

![](images/1b/1b5eadb281202323377386e6b750a304ece8f39232d0c37dc5d4885004a6b588.png)

Similarly, we can also move the graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{x}
$$

to the left or to the right by adding or subtracting a number to the variable $x$ under the square root. For instance, to obtain the graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{x-3}
$$

we perform the following transformations:

- Take the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.
- Translate the graph to the **right** by $3$ units to get the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-3}$.

The result is the solid blue curve shown below.

![](images/6d/6d51b569648468c78445daa6b8dc658fe6e2e8cb24ca8308b60a1f40b07c7e29.png)

Remember:

- Shifting a function up/down/left/right does *not* change the shape of a graph.
- If $a$ is a positive number, then a transformation of the type $y=f(x\pm a)$ is *counter-intuitive*: $f(x+a)$ moves the graph to the *left* by $a$ units, while $f(x-a)$ moves the graph to the *right* by $a$ units." :tutorial/id #uuid "7bdd8c52-b035-531e-b5ba-085731e44771" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4776 :tutorial/title "Vertical and Horizontal Translations"} :step/id #uuid "91171f12-b0b8-5ca8-afcf-bde7eb9fb6fe" :step/math-academy-id 464535 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111662}} {:db/id 17592186111662 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110708 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110531 :question/id #uuid "04070131-1543-5516-a7f1-509ea3f01234" :question/math-academy-id "e-7937"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a70b1e82-4650-5de9-ad47-7578481b802a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048419} {:db/id 17592186050647} {:db/id 17592186050753}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111011} {:db/id 17592186111013}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Square Root Function Containing One Translation"} :step/id #uuid "66c173b6-94ff-5b36-988c-72a5f4e6623b" :step/math-academy-id 464536 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111663}} {:db/id 17592186111663 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110709 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110532 :question/id #uuid "0e964fdb-fa9e-516a-badf-2217a7937bc8" :question/math-academy-id "e-7938"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d3425852-1b32-552e-baaf-bf53644e53b8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111014} {:db/id 17592186111164}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Square Root Function Containing Two Translations"} :step/id #uuid "fd64edda-d116-5987-a423-30af039a0c48" :step/math-academy-id 464539 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111664}} {:db/id 17592186111664 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111896 :tutorial/content "We can reflect the graph of the square root function

$$
y = \sqrt x
$$

in both the $x$ and $y$-axis.

Multiplying the $\sqrt x$ by $-1$ reflects the curve in the $x$-axis. The graph of

$$
y=-\sqrt x
$$

is shown below.

![](images/ee/eef724b522e133a2a537d1b6e1406bdbf17fe285ea43c278888ab4a4bc9fa58c.png)

Multiplying the variable $x$ by $-1$ reflects the curve in the $y$-axis. The graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{-x}
$$

is shown below.

$$

$$

up or down by adding or subtracting a number. For example, to obtain the graph of

$$

![](images/1b/1b5eadb281202323377386e6b750a304ece8f39232d0c37dc5d4885004a6b588.png)

Similarly, we can also move the graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{x}
$$

to the left or to the right by adding or subtracting a number to the variable $x$ under the square root. For instance, to obtain the graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{x-3}
$$

we perform the following transformations:

- Take the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.
- Translate the graph to the **right** by $3$ units to get the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-3}$.

![](images/6d/6d51b569648468c78445daa6b8dc658fe6e2e8cb24ca8308b60a1f40b07c7e29.png)

- Shifting a function up/down/left/right does *not* change the shape of a graph.

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308719 :question/id #uuid "411e1067-1bf2-5810-9a74-3f6443bfc23e" :question/math-academy-id "q-335058" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d9104f75-3823-5343-b10e-35210deee4b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}(4t)" :db/id 17592186307163}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186307163} :answer-field/id #uuid "0de54400-c651-59cf-a2eb-bab2e9e63b82" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307571}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186229133 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228915 :question/id #uuid "c24150ed-748b-5069-9fc5-48d4e6deaef2" :question/math-academy-id "e-21721"} :knowledge-point/id $$

$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).$

$$
y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-At}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$"} {:db/id 17592186311588 :question/id #uuid "8d22d3f6-665f-591f-8d24-fd114ca419a3" $\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ at $t={t}_{0}$ gives

$$
y({t}_{0})={e}^{-A({t}_{0}-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})=Ix({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$

$$

Consider the system

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix, and suppose we are given an initial condition $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$.

Our goal is to derive the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system.

First, we eliminate the *inhomogeneous term* by a change of variables. We define

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t)
$$

and differentiate it using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =\cancel{-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+\cancel{A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate both sides from $t_0$ to $t$ and get

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Next, since $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0),$ we have

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Finally, we convert back to the initial variable $\mathbf{x}(t).$ To do that we multiply both sides by $e^{A(t-t_0)}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our IVP is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where the first term represents the solution of the corresponding *homogeneous system*, and the second term gives a particular solution of our *inhomogeneous system*.

Let's see some concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "ff1bfa7f-286f-5481-8170-effabae1aa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14524 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186229257} {:db/id 17592186229982 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230191 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving *inhomogeneous systems* of ODEs as well. Consider the system

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix, and suppose we are given an initial condition $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$.

Our goal is to derive the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system.

First, we eliminate the *inhomogeneous term* by a change of variables. We define

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t)
$$

and differentiate it using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =\cancel{-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+\cancel{A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate both sides from $t_0$ to $t$ and get

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Next, since $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0),$ we have

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Finally, we convert back to the initial variable $\mathbf{x}(t).$ To do that we multiply both sides by $e^{A(t-t_0)}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our IVP is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where the first term represents the solution of the corresponding *homogeneous system*, and the second term gives a particular solution of our *inhomogeneous system*.

:question/math-academy-id "q-335166" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4x(t)+4,\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>

</tr><tr>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "06d91f07-0fea-5beb-aa8a-cd77b3e6a896" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495188}} {:db/id 17592186495188 :step/content {:db/id 17592186396735 :question/answer-fields ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$
