{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-At}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$"} :step/id #uuid "c5aef665-a069-598d-9521-f09b9a91fe69"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c139fc5d-402e-5c97-b048-caf60e14b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}(2t)-\operatorname{cos}(2t)+3" :db/id 17592186306955} {:answer/id #uuid "6963f53e-90b3-59a4-b3ac-6bc885da9965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\cos(2t)+2\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186494533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494533} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b933995-aeb2-5960-92c8-2edb1a0843a3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307958} {:answer/id #uuid "c139fc5d-402e-5c97-b048-caf60e14b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}(2t)-\operatorname{cos}(2t)+3" :db/id 17592186306955} {:answer/id #uuid "6963f53e-90b3-59a4-b3ac-6bc885da9965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\cos(2t)+2\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186494533} {:db/id 17592186495196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495074 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c02e4fa5-edc3-5680-b383-eb861b94c2ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1" :db/id 17592186494771}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494771} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e66a9d5-c3d1-5ab6-8270-3abb2df59cb7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186494982}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "30dbc074-1ece-5bdf-8ee0-957449e10161" :question/math-academy-id "q-335068" :question/problem "$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=7y(t)+7 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-7x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2fbeaf38-2336-5aee-bfc1-de7e502565a2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495181}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c02e4fa5-edc3-5680-b383-eb861b94c2ae" :answer/type {:db/id \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=2x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=2y(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$*

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4a313e99-6bb3-5fac-9942-cc34685e8d8e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186513010}} {:db/id 17592186513001 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229683 :question/answer-fields $$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).$

$$
y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector.

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ at $t={t}_{0}$ gives

$$
y({t}_{0})={e}^{-A({t}_{0}-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})=Ix({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}(-s+t+1){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-t}-t{e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cef7ab47-7ef6-5ce5-94ff-fd249257c533" :step/next {:db/id 17592186512981}}] :activity/title "Solving Inhomogeneous Systems of ODEs Using Matrix Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186512086} {:db/id 17592186513018 :step/content {:db/id 17592186512945 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-e^{-t}" :db/id 17592186512202}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186512202} :answer-field/id #uuid "7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186512794}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507" :question/math-academy-id "q-335070" :question/problem "$$

$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

|  | $1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1c1ad14e-74e6-51e6-a61f-0245fb4cfb09" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536036}} {:db/id 17592186536026 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311584 :question/answer-fields $$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "98ff146f-1e74-5987-92d5-7e14960c7748" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536026}} {:db/id 17592186536050 :step/content {:db/id 17592186535981 :question/answer-fields \begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "98ff146f-1e74-5987-92d5-7e14960c7748" :step/next {:db/id 17592186536026}} {:db/id 17592186536026 :step/content {:db/id 17592186311584 :question/answer-fields $$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector.

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ -3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -{e}^{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$*

|  | $0$ |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "572e3d09-d0c2-5407-860f-33864b8a2c66"} {:db/id 17592186541191 :step/content {:db/id 17592186229663 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a71f00de-08de-5313-af96-a181750eb6ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t-s}" :db/id 17592186540805}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540805} :answer-field/id #uuid "665a164d-a4b1-5104-b010-c9d2e4fb6aae" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186228180} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ba920ad2-32c3-5075-8ddb-cb1965fbe9d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186540840}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186540840} :answer-field/id #uuid "74529953-db83-50c9-b0ad-3787b4203c7b" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186228181}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5195016b-d389-5c7b-a222-3fb5f86b99aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-334540" :question/problem "$$

Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -{e}^{s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-1)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-1)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -{e}^{s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}

\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-y(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$*

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1-{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "572e3d09-d0c2-5407-860f-33864b8a2c66"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29953a21-209b-586e-a213-f4a4fa9d67d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value use this information to compute the common difference of the sequence?

The first thing to note is that the sequence is *increasing*, and therefore we expect the common difference $d$ to be positive.

Now, let's take a look at the jumps:

![](images/6b/6b82ba58c986aa32635e2ebbd8b1e0fd0affdbc81e35a015960777fa72d5f72b.png)

Because $a_4 = 6$ and $a_5 = 12$ are **consecutive terms**, meaning that $a_5$ comes straight after $a_4$ in the sequence, we can easily compute the common difference $d$ by subtracting $a_4$ from $a_5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{5}-{a}_{4} \\  & =12-6 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e69a6b27-01d4-5ee2-81c3-d7d8f834b087" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8911 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d8a0caf7-c1c8-5350-9d6b-8db3c51bdd00" :step/math-academy-id 148381 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079293}} {:db/id 17592186079293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078423 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078183 :question/id #uuid "cb23119e-7625-5dad-873f-03049677618c" :question/math-academy-id "e-14385"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9307a5e-2eea-5cea-b5f3-2ce6df53961e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049579}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078779} {:db/id 17592186078787} {:db/id 17592186079080} {:db/id 17592186519529} {:db/id 17592186519564} {:db/id 17592186519575}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Common Difference Given Two Consecutive Terms"} :step/id #uuid "ca7d2f7b-9202-580e-bad9-b64525e020c2" :step/math-academy-id 148382 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079294}} {:db/id 17592186079294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079729 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the second and fifth terms only of an arithmetic sequence. For example, suppose that we know that

$$
a_2 = {\color{red}8}, \quad a_5 = {\color{red}23}
$$

These terms are not consecutive, and so how can we figure out the common difference $d?$

First, let's take a look at the jumps:

![](images/ff/ff83c75935acca7ddd5c421cd81fad85685c68fd782d1d832c068237c751753d.png)

We see that between ${\color{red}8}$ and ${\color{red}23}$, there are a total of ${\color{blue}3}$ jumps. So, to find the value of a single jump, we can take the total difference and divide it by the number of jumps:

$$
d = \frac{{\color{red}23}\,-\,{\color{red}8}}{\color{blue}3} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5
$$

We can check that our result $d=5$ is correct by using it to figure out the intermediate terms. Indeed, the common difference $d=5$ gets us from $a_2={\color{red}8}$ to $a_5={\color{red}23}$ in ${\color{blue}3}$ jumps:

![](images/7a/7aa192675aeb3c7be78617035b74362b38974e8501d95c0692238811ae4769f1.png)

In general, if we're given two terms $a_n$ and $a_m$ of an arithmetic sequence, then we can calculate the common difference using the following formula:

$$
d = \frac{a_n-a_m}{n-m}
$$

Using this formula to calculate the common difference between $a_{2}=8$ and $a_{5}=23,$ we get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{5}-{a}_{2}}{5-2} \\  & =\frac{23-8}{5-2} \\  & =\frac{15}{3} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dab8ebfb-480a-5a36-9a12-169a69cd8316" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8913 :tutorial/title "Non-Consecutive Terms"} :step/id #uuid "59dd0405-0ca2-5664-bbd2-78d0a305318e" :step/math-academy-id 148386 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079295}} {:db/id 17592186079295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078424 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078185 :question/id #uuid "a22637f2-14e5-55ff-a41b-1f2a7e0eaa73" :question/math-academy-id "e-14390"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4d15f023-4061-51ad-b307-013bd06d3ec1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048938}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078772} {:db/id 17592186078788} {:db/id 17592186078789} {:db/id 17592186519596} {:db/id 17592186519606}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Common Difference Given Two Non-Consecutive Terms"} :step/id #uuid "2f2df9f7-ad2a-5436-aa72-25df975ccb0b" :step/math-academy-id 148387}] :activity/title "Finding the Common Difference of an Arithmetic Sequence" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186078685} {:db/id 17592186079292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079728 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the fourth term of an arithmetic sequence is $6$ and the fifth term is $12.$ Can we use this information to compute the common difference of the sequence?

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y+1,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ Find $b$ given that $a=1.$" :question/worked-solution "According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b)\in D$ such that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=f(a,b)\cdot \text{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+2y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}+2y+1)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}+y]_{y=0}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{3}+12x]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =({2}^{3}+12\cdot 2)-0 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\text{Area}(D)=2\cdot 3=6.
$$

Also, we are told that $a=1.$ So, our initial equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}32 & =f(1,b)\cdot 6 \\ 32 & =({1}^{2}+2b+1)\cdot 6 \\ 32 & =12b+12 \\ 20 & =12b \\ b & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $(1,\frac{5}{3})\in D.$ Therefore, the answer is $b=\frac{5}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186167133 :question/id #uuid "a40ddcf2-e6e2-5966-908e-b51c9f5915b1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163060" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166883 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d13b0d31-65b8-550f-b97b-f4ece63bf834" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aec11462-7527-5c1f-bee1-5311de75df3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186163877} {:answer/id #uuid "28a5d564-3fad-5bcd-bbd4-8313b0c26770" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186163878} {:answer/id #uuid "41a558e9-c044-57fc-99da-3a88324c2b3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186163879} {:answer/id #uuid "5336652c-5f4b-557f-994b-7062409121b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186163880} {:answer/id #uuid "667f6b41-1da3-5dde-85af-5f6ba8248df0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186163881}] :answer-field/id #uuid "91ed5a91-8a47-5da8-b4fa-8f64aaacc1c1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186163876}] :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x, y)$ and the region $D$ given by

$f(x,y)=2x+y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/b5/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2}=2\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{8}{3\pi }.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281588 :question/id #uuid "636e23a3-a873-5229-81ee-5d1161e02dcd" :question/math-academy-id "q-163070"} {:db/id 17592186281653 :question/id #uuid "9470a948-0cd8-55e7-86d6-65b250b7e800" :question/math-academy-id "q-163260"} {:db/id 17592186281654 :question/id #uuid "9c6dbd46-16b0-53ac-9c25-a6637f9ce3ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-163261"} {:db/id 17592186281662 :question/id #uuid "4da84d34-65b6-5264-9689-a8f568b0485b" :question/math-academy-id "q-163278" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27060319-319a-5c93-87a4-021b464e69b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186278938} {:answer/id #uuid "96cddbff-aa96-5c15-b451-85bc3b5899ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186279926} {:answer/id #uuid "d6297845-0a0a-51e3-9056-3d94de569441" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186280482} {:answer/id #uuid "d932caf8-3377-5328-b82d-2c72ffe1d077" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186280511} {:answer/id #uuid "fb6871d0-cf0d-5786-9a5c-fd24e0463ae0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{5\pi }" :db/id 17592186280794}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280794} :answer-field/id #uuid "d4bf3c23-4651-531a-8ea1-05778a87081e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281209}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/f8/f84a8fcd4ed668a6b94d5b084ade49dc8fc027feff4baea862e2feaf68221534.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(-1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x} \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{[-\frac{{cos}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}({cos}^{5}⁡\pi -{cos}^{5}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot \frac{4}{5}=\frac{8}{5\pi }.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281663 :question/id #uuid "128ce1a7-9b5d-51fb-9a3d-78ee6a5214c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163279"} {:db/id 17592186374241 :question/id #uuid "75bad8c5-dff2-5d67-88eb-d6d0bf7d0cd9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163258"} {:db/id 17592186411860 :question/id #uuid "5ff06561-72e7-5575-b3f6-d0740b1e717f" :question/math-academy-id "q-163259"} {:db/id 17592186481357 :question/id #uuid "3b9226c2-67e0-5858-9c64-ae46c4147a95" :question/math-academy-id "q-163257" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7e360105-eb66-5367-814d-689677702f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186480975} {:answer/id #uuid "9e9f7126-1aec-56cb-a084-4f34d28dafc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186481043} {:answer/id #uuid "a79440e4-ebcc-5811-a667-c1e64c7db96b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186481055} {:answer/id #uuid "c27b400b-e962-57cc-9be7-11f6f93220fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186481111} {:answer/id #uuid "d99527b4-de43-5d96-9eda-144ff935847e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481146}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480975} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a10b6cc-8155-5c1e-bf70-aecfcd94d2ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481254}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$ on the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

*Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c77b7ad4-9d8d-58f4-bd79-4c0b0b47cfea" :step/content {:db/id 17592186168150 :tutorial/content "Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

 

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

*If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

 

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "b65eeb5f-8a44-55b9-819c-1c6c0d979d1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7778 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "037c5a22-eee3-557c-b683-370d2389ad82" :step/math-academy-id 45031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167795}} {:db/id 17592186167795 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168151 :tutorial/content "Consider the continuous function 

$$
f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2
$$

and the region $D$ given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation describes part of a parabola in the $xy$-plane, as shown below.

![](images/46/46873c4ecb290380488e589082fc0759324d3540494f5b83e2d64db5d9cdf62a.png)

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c77b7ad4-9d8d-58f4-bd79-4c0b0b47cfea" :step/math-academy-id 44981 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167792}} {:db/id 17592186168149 :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

*Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*

$$
f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} {:db/id 17592186167792 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166884 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166489 :question/id #uuid "0a06a8ae-69d6-5ded-979e-149f650a1676" :question/math-academy-id "e-12491"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b43eea5b-9da3-5fe0-a28c-cc01aed3627a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167134} {:db/id 17592186167135} {:db/id 17592186235532} {:db/id 17592186281645} {:db/id 17592186281646} {:db/id 17592186281649} {:db/id 17592186281652} {:db/id 17592186374220} {:db/id 17592186374227} {:db/id 17592186374234} {:db/id 17592186481348} {:db/id 17592186481402} {:db/id 17592186481411}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c0151bcd-ba24-5681-9ec6-52888fa06a36" :step/math-academy-id 44982 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167793}} {:db/id 17592186167793 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166885 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166490 :question/id #uuid "13800660-08b4-50af-93b4-1013bbf41e66" :question/math-academy-id "e-12492"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c4e5deee-e910-5bb1-9d9a-0b24886ab6c1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049084}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167136} {:db/id 17592186167137} {:db/id 17592186281588} {:db/id 17592186281653} {:db/id 17592186281654} {:db/id 17592186281662} {:db/id 17592186281663} {:db/id 17592186374241} {:db/id 17592186411860} {:db/id 17592186481357} {:db/id 17592186481407} {:db/id 17592186481408}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Average Value of a Function Over a Polar Region"} :step/id #uuid "a1446b8a-1f48-5f9e-b01f-42db997299c2" :step/math-academy-id 44985} {:db/id 17592186168150 :tutorial/content "Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

 

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

*If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

 

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "b65eeb5f-8a44-55b9-819c-1c6c0d979d1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7778 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186167795 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168151 :tutorial/content "Consider the continuous function 

$$
f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2
$$

and the region $D$ given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation describes part of a parabola in the $xy$-plane, as shown below.

![](images/46/46873c4ecb290380488e589082fc0759324d3540494f5b83e2d64db5d9cdf62a.png)

  

To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, $b=1 \in [0,2]$ and obtain $a=2.$ So, the point $(2,1)$ satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume.

![](images/82/82d3a762ab323339570e6010038e75ce95f3fdbde958a2ffa876972cbf91e8fb.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "b890c915-3364-5ac3-b88b-298ed92d9def" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7784 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "32b5b570-9467-5bff-bc3b-29964ed86c09" :step/math-academy-id 45050 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167790}} {:db/id 17592186168151 :tutorial/content "Consider the continuous function
