![](images/82/82d3a762ab323339570e6010038e75ce95f3fdbde958a2ffa876972cbf91e8fb.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "b890c915-3364-5ac3-b88b-298ed92d9def" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7784 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186538051} :activity/id #uuid "119140e4-3b93-53de-ab7b-40456eb040a1" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049957 :topic/id #uuid "21390ce8-05ac-5fcf-ba45-89cb6f33aadc" :topic/math-academy-id 3147} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186538006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186481357 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7e360105-eb66-5367-814d-689677702f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186480975} {:answer/id #uuid "9e9f7126-1aec-56cb-a084-4f34d28dafc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186481043} {:answer/id #uuid "a79440e4-ebcc-5811-a667-c1e64c7db96b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186481055} {:answer/id #uuid "c27b400b-e962-57cc-9be7-11f6f93220fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186481111} {:answer/id #uuid "d99527b4-de43-5d96-9eda-144ff935847e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481146}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480975} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a10b6cc-8155-5c1e-bf70-aecfcd94d2ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481254}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3b9226c2-67e0-5858-9c64-ae46c4147a95" :question/math-academy-id "q-163257" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$ on the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{4\pi }\cdot 4\pi =1.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3418e5df-6b11-57d2-bb99-1913431eb137" :step/next {:db/id 17592186538057}} {:db/id 17592186538032 :step/content {:db/id 17592186481411 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b7b96a3-3ee8-51d8-bf7e-f10bc137dc77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186480796} {:answer/id #uuid "5ea1906a-4d23-5e92-aa42-2516002c4c66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186480915} {:answer/id #uuid "654022a5-61f4-581f-8b07-c11340a40a55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186480925} {:answer/id #uuid "e98d6b52-9796-58a4-ba09-031961cb2020" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186481186} {:answer/id #uuid "fc2a60a5-710d-5d16-938e-a0bd54aeac9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186481227}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480925} :answer-field/id #uuid "da8ec83a-e269-5c73-bf54-b07a27aefc49" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bbfd9077-09aa-55c5-a7ec-ce238f7922af" :question/math-academy-id "q-163240" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y+{x}^{2}$ on the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2x\}$ given that the area of the region is $2.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{D}y+{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2x}y+{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}y]_{y=x}^{y=2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{x}^{3}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}]\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}]_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(8-0) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "876ec9b0-fca4-5f08-ab51-9230e03dee9c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186538069}} {:db/id 17592186538051 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167137 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c1ea06c-900b-518b-90c1-188a82af18c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186163902} {:answer/id #uuid "4486d7e0-2a87-59a4-9e31-7eb1fae5055e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{3}" :db/id 17592186163904} {:answer/id #uuid "3243821a-d8ad-5dd7-aced-e15740550519" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186480836} {:answer/id #uuid "932abe94-bffd-5dad-a100-ed7dd0878970" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186481015} {:answer/id #uuid "a461f542-25f5-59e6-a3ba-329bd57b7ee7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186481048}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481015} :answer-field/id #uuid "a885e1f2-0379-5509-836d-b0ab6acba537" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186163900}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e7ccaa25-bf49-56f7-93ee-b9d797d03126" :question/math-academy-id "q-163068" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/b5/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2}=2\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{8}{3\pi }.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bd571a32-8693-5c5f-99bb-0070c9bb2fcd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186538032}} {:db/id 17592186538057 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281662 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27060319-319a-5c93-87a4-021b464e69b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186278938} {:answer/id #uuid "96cddbff-aa96-5c15-b451-85bc3b5899ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186279926} {:answer/id #uuid "d6297845-0a0a-51e3-9056-3d94de569441" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186280482} {:answer/id #uuid "d932caf8-3377-5328-b82d-2c72ffe1d077" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8\pi }{5}" :db/id 17592186280511} {:answer/id #uuid "fb6871d0-cf0d-5786-9a5c-fd24e0463ae0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{5\pi }" :db/id 17592186280794}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280794} :answer-field/id #uuid "d4bf3c23-4651-531a-8ea1-05778a87081e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281209}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4da84d34-65b6-5264-9689-a8f568b0485b" :question/math-academy-id "q-163278" :question/problem "![](images/f8/f84a8fcd4ed668a6b94d5b084ade49dc8fc027feff4baea862e2feaf68221534.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(-1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x} \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{[-\frac{{cos}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}({cos}^{5}⁡\pi -{cos}^{5}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot \frac{4}{5}=\frac{8}{5\pi }.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cb0bae8e-56e4-5d43-8dbc-3436ea5c01f1"} {:db/id 17592186538069 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281649 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1c9c1a55-bba0-56ad-b34a-3f8e8d7f257c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186278854} {:answer/id #uuid "626dc16f-8c1c-5295-aa50-90b66258e711" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186279486} {:answer/id #uuid "67ad624f-1636-5880-94a3-08d7d29a2390" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186279534} {:answer/id #uuid "d1e6422b-62b6-59e0-932d-a0c2aeb5b3e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186280446} {:answer/id #uuid "d4cb2768-4bcd-5b37-aeef-50e75f09d3ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186280468}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279486} :answer-field/id #uuid "08429d71-a216-5cf2-b30e-790877dfd6fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280845}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "94920c42-c29f-5248-bff0-1bbc9f005b27" :question/math-academy-id "q-163246" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=2x+3{y}^{2}$ on the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=1\cdot 2=2.
$$

Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{ave}} & =\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{D}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2xy+{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4x+8)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[2{x}^{2}+8x]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot {1}^{2}+8\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{10}{2} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "f52a63f9-5aaf-58b5-bc92-454c75b1e996" :step/next {:db/id 17592186538006}}] :activity/title "The Average Value of a Multivariable Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186537205} {:db/id 17592186538051 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167137 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c1ea06c-900b-518b-90c1-188a82af18c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186163902} {:answer/id #uuid "4486d7e0-2a87-59a4-9e31-7eb1fae5055e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16}{3}" :db/id 17592186163904} {:answer/id #uuid "3243821a-d8ad-5dd7-aced-e15740550519" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{\pi }" :db/id 17592186480836} {:answer/id #uuid "932abe94-bffd-5dad-a100-ed7dd0878970" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186481015} {:answer/id #uuid "a461f542-25f5-59e6-a3ba-329bd57b7ee7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3\pi }" :db/id 17592186481048}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481015} :answer-field/id #uuid "a885e1f2-0379-5509-836d-b0ab6acba537" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186163900}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e7ccaa25-bf49-56f7-93ee-b9d797d03126" :question/math-academy-id "q-163068" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y$ on the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch our region $D:$ 

![](images/b5/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

Notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2}=2\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{2\pi }\cdot \frac{16}{3}=\frac{8}{3\pi }.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bd571a32-8693-5c5f-99bb-0070c9bb2fcd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186538032}} {:db/id 17592186538006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186481357 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7e360105-eb66-5367-814d-689677702f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186480975} {:answer/id #uuid "9e9f7126-1aec-56cb-a084-4f34d28dafc8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186481043} {:answer/id #uuid "a79440e4-ebcc-5811-a667-c1e64c7db96b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186481055} {:answer/id #uuid "c27b400b-e962-57cc-9be7-11f6f93220fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186481111} {:answer/id #uuid "d99527b4-de43-5d96-9eda-144ff935847e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186481146}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480975} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a10b6cc-8155-5c1e-bf70-aecfcd94d2ca" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481254}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3b9226c2-67e0-5858-9c64-ae46c4147a95" :question/math-academy-id "q-163257" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$ on the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi .
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (4-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{[\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =2[(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)] \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-163278" :question/problem "![](images/f8/f84a8fcd4ed668a6b94d5b084ade49dc8fc027feff4baea862e2feaf68221534.png)

Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ on the semicircle shown above." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
\text{Area}(D)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {1}^{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The average value of the function over a region $D$ is given by

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\,{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(-1,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-2x} \\ {y}^{2} & =-{x}^{2}-2x \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-2x \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ((-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{4}-{0}^{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{[-\frac{{cos}^{5}⁡\theta }{5}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}({cos}^{5}⁡\pi -{cos}^{5}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{f}_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}\cdot \frac{4}{5}=\frac{8}{5\pi }.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cb0bae8e-56e4-5d43-8dbc-3436ea5c01f1"} {:db/id 17592186538032 :step/content {:db/id 17592186481411 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b7b96a3-3ee8-51d8-bf7e-f10bc137dc77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186480796} {:answer/id #uuid "5ea1906a-4d23-5e92-aa42-2516002c4c66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186480915} {:answer/id #uuid "654022a5-61f4-581f-8b07-c11340a40a55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186480925} {:answer/id #uuid "e98d6b52-9796-58a4-ba09-031961cb2020" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186481186} {:answer/id #uuid "fc2a60a5-710d-5d16-938e-a0bd54aeac9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186481227}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186480925} :answer-field/id #uuid "da8ec83a-e269-5c73-bf54-b07a27aefc49" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186481322}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bbfd9077-09aa-55c5-a7ec-ce238f7922af" :question/math-academy-id "q-163240" :question/problem "Find the average value of the function $f(x,y)=y+{x}^{2}$ on the region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2x\}$ given that the area of the region is $2.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

$$

$$
d=2\cdot r=2\cdot 6=12.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2x-1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}.\end{aligned}

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186524983 :question/id #uuid "45936e93-e188-5489-9cc9-795dad15e0d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-342792"} {:db/id 17592186542130 :question/id #uuid "316d8b52-05f5-5660-9987-6f2357a674ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-342789" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "496974f1-cd7b-5abe-b03b-8caf3c2ef7ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186541574}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541574} :answer-field/id #uuid "6df6c47b-c813-591d-800c-7da989a956a4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186542020}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}$ at the point where $x=1$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-{x}^{2}+2x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-2x+2) \\  & =\frac{-2x+2}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{-2x+2}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{-2(1)+2}{2\sqrt{-{1}^{2}+2(1)}} \\  & =\frac{0}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186542221 :question/id #uuid "ed421aa6-2e1d-544f-a145-c01b981f6e83" :question/math-academy-id "q-20181" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "365d6570-d8cb-539f-a88f-8f59a136deaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{145}{2}" :db/id 17592186541535} {:answer/id #uuid "a8e65a94-bc73-5511-b4e0-737b7fd4a52d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{2}" :db/id 17592186541771} {:answer/id #uuid "ba942dc9-148d-5089-895a-5986590e89c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{289}{2}" :db/id 17592186541806} {:answer/id #uuid "dfa31f6a-0231-55ef-b7c1-eda435cc6895" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{73}{2}" :db/id 17592186541897} {:answer/id #uuid "fb45a9d2-d3cd-5774-a7e6-b9653552ab14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{33}{2}" :db/id 17592186541949}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541806} :answer-field/id #uuid "02bb9c7f-0a51-5ad4-a60d-65bfb06add50" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186541965}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{x-3}+3{x}^{3}$ at the point where $x=4.$" :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=x-3.$ Then $f=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the sum rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-3}}+9{x}^{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=4} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4-3}}+9(4)^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+144 \\  & =\frac{289}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$"} {:db/id 17592186049332} {:db/id 17592186050271} {:db/id 17592186050628} {:db/id 17592186050789} {:activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186097783} :activity/id #uuid "00c1cd54-a7af-5240-860b-4432978fec0c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186051084 :topic/id #uuid "7fcc3a06-676a-55a2-9979-d3726053babe" :topic/math-academy-id 1108} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097750 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097807 :tutorial/content "Let's now prove the chain rule in the following form:

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = f'(g(a)) \cdot g'(a)
$$

Let $f$ and $g$ be functions such that

- $g$ is differentiable at $a$,

- $f$ is differentiable at $g(a)$.

Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $a$, and we compute its derivative as follows.

We start with the definition of the derivative:

$$
(f \circ g)'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a}
$$

Since $g$ is differentiable at $a$, it is also continuous there. Hence $g(x) \to g(a)$ as $x \to a$. For $x$ sufficiently close to $a$, we have $g(x) \ne g(a)$, so we may write

$$
\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{x - a} 
= \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(a))}{g(x) - g(a)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(a)}{x - a}.
$$

Taking the limit as $x \to a$, and using the product rule for limits (which applies since both limits exist), we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(f∘g)^{′}(a) & ={lim}_{x\to a}(\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot \frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(g(x))-f(g(a))}{g(x)-g(a)}\cdot {lim}_{x\to a}\frac{g(x)-g(a)}{x-a} \\  & ={f}^{′}(g(a))\cdot {g}^{′}(a)\end{aligned}
$$

as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "d34fc877-5572-53a2-b957-2c5d44a488f3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13330 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Chain Rule"} :step/id #uuid "9ad2def5-511c-587f-9847-fa7af8e06405" :step/math-academy-id 466057} {:db/id 17592186097783 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097872 :tutorial/content "The **chain rule** for differentiation states that the derivative of a composite function $f(g(x))$ is given by

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac {\textrm{d}f} {\textrm{d}g} \cdot \dfrac {\textrm{d}g} {\textrm{d}x}.
$$

There is some intuition behind this rule: if we think of the derivatives as fractions, the ${\textrm{d}g}$'s would appear to cancel out.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\cancel{\text{d}g}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\text{d}g}}{\text{d}x}\end{aligned}
$$

To see how the chain rule can be used to differentiate a function like 

$$
f(x) = (1+2x)^3,
$$

first, notice that the function can be written as a composite function

$$
f(g) = g^3, \qquad g(x) = 1+2x.
$$

We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}g}({g}^{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+2x) \\  & =3{g}^{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =6{g}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(x) = 1+2x$ for $g,$ we obtain the final result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =6(1+2x)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We'll provide a derivation of the chain rule at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "743ad997-8732-5c0f-9676-ff1d44f3b513" :tutorial/math-academy-id 415 :tutorial/title $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =8{g}^{7}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-24(1-3x)^{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4350c72e-f9bd-5210-90fd-d37e9cc293c0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520579}} {:db/id 17592186520551 :step/content {:db/id 17592186520516 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "33c7c493-bcdb-5703-aa16-7951eec23ed2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186520068}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520068} :answer-field/id #uuid "3b694189-fec1-5a06-8456-a524e215acf6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186520382}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fa666076-05a3-50c7-be3d-b7a39d6d4f55" :question/math-academy-id "q-314192" :question/problem "The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{4x+1}$ at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=4x+1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={(\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4x+1}})|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(0)+1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "51f59503-df73-54cc-af64-3dcb163fe7d6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186520538}} {:db/id 17592186520579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186520487 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "454a250f-2e0e-5eff-ad08-2e1a4569c3b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520091} {:answer/id #uuid "4cf36f6a-ac30-5d76-9499-88f79530ef58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520108} {:answer/id #uuid "a63c2527-a87a-5317-bb52-435b49980a68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520218} {:answer/id #uuid "ceae46e6-5020-51b1-a35e-422b64ddda99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520281} {:answer/id #uuid "edcc6c31-a212-5340-8bdb-e1b0f8c22746" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2x-1}}" :db/id 17592186520341}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520091} :answer-field/id #uuid "7e463a5a-0bf7-5c15-8a84-e8fb513aab4c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186520404}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "98cde390-f268-5ffd-9f2f-31f016a0c432" :question/math-academy-id "q-107303" :question/problem "Given that $y=\sqrt{2x-1},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$" :question/worked-solution "We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2x-1.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =({g}^{5})^{′}=5{g}^{4}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(4x+3)^{′}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =5{g}^{4}\cdot (4) \\  & =20(4x+3)^{4}.\end{aligned}

#uuid "316d8b52-05f5-5660-9987-6f2357a674ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-342789" :question/problem "The slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}$ at the point where $x=1$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-{x}^{2}+2x.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x+2.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-2x+2) \\  & =\frac{-2x+2}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{-2x+2}{2\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x}})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{-2(1)+2}{2\sqrt{-{1}^{2}+2(1)}} \\  & =\frac{0}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "dd09ffd1-587d-547b-937b-c610cc67ad37" :step/next {:db/id 17592186542241}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "496974f1-cd7b-5abe-b03b-8caf3c2ef7ba" :answer/type {:db/id Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns $\mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of $q_{11} \cdot r_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ![](images/71/714ad80d47ea58159e0e486f5bfc5a6657fd441bc47aa2b8fa7230a89bdb0445.svg)

**Step 2**. We find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\frac{12}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-2\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{6} & 2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{12}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}-(-\frac{12}{6})\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{6} & -2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -3\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{6} & -2\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & \sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}}}.
$$

\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]-\frac{24}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & 4\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & 4\sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{12}\cdot {r}_{22}=(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})\cdot (4\sqrt{3})=-4.$"} {:db/id 17592186510452 :question/id #uuid "ca2de93c-f55b-512e-9e27-ab6ff5bd3cb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-96041" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133798 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "19ae0632-68ac-5da9-8adf-cf71d5ecbc7c" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the QR Factorization of a Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "072eda89-f2fd-5e6b-8865-e919b2deb069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186509707} {:answer/id #uuid "6acfb0da-27b6-5749-b6e8-62595ebc8056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186509908} {:answer/id #uuid "7cce974d-ff76-5e44-b28b-aec2865278ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186509957} {:answer/id #uuid "9557cf45-32ca-5990-b9e7-8944ea966b53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186510002} {:answer/id #uuid "a3b55a48-54cb-5cad-b04e-d24581a88559" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186510028}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "9557cf45-32ca-5990-b9e7-8944ea966b53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186510002} :answer-field/id #uuid "36df5534-c619-54f6-902b-ac3c15f3e762" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186510267}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{6}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=2.$"} {:db/id 17592186133821 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133633 :question/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{2}\,⟹\,{v}_{1}=2{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{3}\,⟹\,{v}_{2}=3{q}_{2} \\ {q}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{4}\,⟹\,{v}_{3}=4{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the set $\big\{ \mathbf{q}_1,\mathbf{q}_2,\mathbf{q}_3 \big\}$ will be both orthogonal and normalized.

Next, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$

![](images/f5/f53a5eb3b2d24ad186382f8eed42775b2ee61d34a20a0af821a38c17d846e873.svg)

![](images/27/2797cd9e375b3a28f3f8afc8c49b85e202ad5cc87fb5a332ebb9abd73f388ee3.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
r_{13}+r_{23}+r_{33} = 6+(-6)+4 = 4.

\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | \\ \frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖} & \frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖} & \frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖} \\ | & | & |\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}{r}_{11} & {r}_{12} & {r}_{13} \\ 0 & {r}_{22} & {r}_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & {r}_{33}\end{bmatrix}}}
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above, where $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is an orthogonal set of vectors. You're given that $‖{v}_{1}‖=4,$ $‖{v}_{2}‖=2,$ $‖{v}_{3}‖=6,$ and that the system of equations below describes the relationship between the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A.$ 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} &={a}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} &={a}_{2}-2{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{3} &={a}_{3}-4{v}_{1}+3{v}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

What is the value of ${r}_{11}+{r}_{13}+{r}_{33}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we normalize the vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{4}\,⟹\,{v}_{1}=4{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{2}\,⟹\,{v}_{2}=2{q}_{2} \\ {q}_{3} & =\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{6}\,⟹\,{v}_{3}=6{q}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the set $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{3}\}$ will be both orthogonal and normalized.

Next, let's rewrite the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ as a linear combination of the vectors ${q}_{1},{q}_{2},{q}_{3}:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} &={a}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} &={a}_{2}-2{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{3} &={a}_{3}-4{v}_{1}+3{v}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} &={v}_{1}=4{q}_{1} \\ {a}_{2} &=2{v}_{1}+{v}_{2}=8{q}_{1}+2{q}_{2} \\ {a}_{3} &=4{v}_{1}-3{v}_{2}+{v}_{3}=16{q}_{1}-6{q}_{2}+6{q}_{3}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The final system can be written in matrix form as follows:

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & {a}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}| & | & | \\ {q}_{1} & {q}_{2} & {q}_{3} \\ | & | & |\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}4 & 8 & 16 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix}}}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{r}_{11}+{r}_{13}+{r}_{33}=4+16+6=26.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186363217 :question/id #uuid "9d67166f-3bff-552c-8a7c-19cfbf3fd7f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-140900"} {:db/id 17592186364171 :question/id #uuid "e0bac4d5-3752-5a5d-b6fe-39c8ef101bd9" :question/math-academy-id "q-41485"} {:db/id 17592186364178 :question/id #uuid "0711fb88-caa5-5f45-81df-dbacaf0d183c" :question/math-academy-id "q-41486" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133821 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cd18abf3-b551-55d6-a573-690745a65b3e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a QR Factorization of a Matrix Given an Orthogonal Basis in Terms of the Columns of a Matrix"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "74849d77-3f75-57fb-9eda-c7eb146ef089" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186364180} {:answer/id #uuid "ae17bbad-6406-590f-9037-515c2d2e3302" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186364181} {:answer/id #uuid "80193887-56ef-5f55-9899-81a4ca2a5bfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186364182} {:answer/id #uuid "d9ed3821-6db7-500c-afa6-af890beb1af8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186364183} {:answer/id #uuid "ee368a24-e35e-5530-bc4c-c0b11699a84f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186364184}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "80193887-56ef-5f55-9899-81a4ca2a5bfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186364182} :answer-field/id #uuid "bfd9129a-1c55-5b4e-92c4-8f9a2d89199f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186364179}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$

$$

[{:db/id 17592186133864 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1304189f-61ac-53c5-9b09-8e365f763136" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Dimensions of Factors in a QR Factorization"}] :question/problem "Given that $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of a $3 \times 2$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, which of the following statements are true?

I. $Q$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix

II. The columns of $Q$ form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)$

III. $R$ is an upper triangular matrix" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if $A=QR$ is a QR factorization of an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ then

$$
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{A}
=
\underset{{\large m} \times {\large n}}{Q} \times \underset{{\large n} \times {\large n}}{R},
$$

where 

- $Q$ is an $m \times n$ matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)$

- $R$ is an $n \times n$ upper triangular matrix

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

{:db/id 17592186134801 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135097 :tutorial/content "Given the matrix $Q$ in the QR factorization of an $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ how do we find $R?$

Recall that $Q$ has orthonormal columns, so pre-multiplying both sides of $A=QR$ by $Q^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}\cdot A & ={Q}^{T}\cdot QR \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={Q}^{T}QR.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note that since the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal we have $Q^TQ = I_n.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}^{T}A & =({Q}^{T}Q)R \\ {Q}^{T}A & ={I}_{n}R \\ R & ={Q}^{T}A.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can find $R$ by pre-multiplying $A$ by the transpose of $Q.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "20b6ab0a-cf41-550b-9242-2bb3f84c4917" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5017 :tutorial/title "Computing the Matrix R Given the Matrix Q in a QR Factorization"} :step/id #uuid "eebb9689-f8b3-55e2-8167-e5f5525e382a" :step/math-academy-id 31388 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134798}} {:db/id 17592186134802 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135098 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown below:

![](images/ee/ee731d95c111101559ad135429198dd7e0b14313272f0933b1c706006da2fbd2.svg)

Suppose also that we are given the following system of equations that connects the columns of $Q$ and the columns of $A{:}$  

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} &=\frac{1}{2}{a}_{1} \\ {q}_{2} &=\frac{1}{3}{a}_{2}+3{q}_{1} \\ {q}_{3} &=\frac{1}{4}{a}_{3}-2{q}_{1}+{q}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

How do we find $R?$
First, let's rewrite the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ as a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \mathbf{q}_3 \mathbin{:}$
![](images/82/824c39c97bb115768856d672b39be8f65d8b4ecbc2ee5d6ccc9f4943594cbacd.svg)

In this new system, the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_1$ correspond to the first-row entries of $R,$ the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_2$ correspond to the second-row entries of $R,$ and the coefficients of $\mathbf{q}_3$ correspond to the third-row entries of $R.$ Therefore,

![](images/5b/5ba9887a4d9b47963af171e9275319a2564eca5a4ef8b3ef44978e2ff4b111d9.svg)

To see why this is, we can take the transpose of both sides of $A=QR{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =QR \\ {A}^{T} & =(QR)^{T} \\ {A}^{T} & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T} \\ \overset{{A}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-\,\,\,\, & {a}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {a}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{bmatrix}}} & =\overset{{R}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 8 & -4 & 4\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}-\,\,\,\, & {q}_{1} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{2} & \,\,\,\,- \\ -\,\,\,\, & {q}_{3} & \,\,\,\,-\end{bmatrix}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we were to expand this matrix product, we would obtain our system of equations." :tutorial/id #uuid "9a6d9a3e-33d4-52e8-b8b0-98cd20590dd6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5018 :tutorial/title "Interpreting Relations Between Two Bases as Matrix Multiplication"} :step/id #uuid "fdc0053f-e37d-51ef-835e-365ca5c6da98" :step/math-academy-id 31389 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134732}} {:db/id 17592186134803 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135099 :tutorial/content "Let's now go through the QR factorization algorithm to find the factorization of the matrix

![](images/f0/f0d468f6bce43491b3f97d10185f4393ae8e64198e24bb7708ad66ec57c73df4.svg)

**Step 1**. Orthogonalize the columns of $A$ to get the columns of $Q.$ Using the Gram-Schmidt process, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\,{q}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**. Compute $R=Q^TA.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}R=\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{6}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ 0 & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\end{bmatrix}}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{6}\end{bmatrix}}}
$$

Finally, ${q}_{32}\cdot {r}_{22}=-\frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot \sqrt{6}=-2.$"} :step/id #uuid "8870d163-7037-5417-a28f-0af8d578e0cb"} {:db/id 17592186510538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186510452 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "072eda89-f2fd-5e6b-8865-e919b2deb069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186509707} {:answer/id #uuid "6acfb0da-27b6-5749-b6e8-62595ebc8056" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186509908} {:answer/id #uuid "7cce974d-ff76-5e44-b28b-aec2865278ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186509957} {:answer/id #uuid "9557cf45-32ca-5990-b9e7-8944ea966b53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186510002} {:answer/id #uuid "a3b55a48-54cb-5cad-b04e-d24581a88559" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186510028}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186510002} :answer-field/id #uuid "36df5534-c619-54f6-902b-ac3c15f3e762" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186510267}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "ca2de93c-f55b-512e-9e27-ab6ff5bd3cb0" :question/math-academy-id "q-96041" :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the QR factorization of the matrix $A$ shown above. Given that the columns ${q}_{1},{q}_{2}$ of $Q$ were obtained from the columns of $A$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, find  the value of ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ be the columns of $A.$

First, we find an orthonormal basis of $\text{Col}(A)=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ using the Gram-Schmidt process.

**Step 1**. We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**. We find the vector ${v}_{2}$ orthogonal to $\text{Span}\{{v}_{1}\}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{6}{12}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we normalize ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {q}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}R & ={Q}^{T}\,A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following QR factorization of $A:$

$$
\overset{A}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}=\overset{Q}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & 0\end{aligned}]}}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3} & \sqrt{3} \\ 0 & 2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}.
$$

Finally, ${q}_{22}\cdot {r}_{22}=(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=2.$"} :step/id #uuid "ba9899ad-e46c-5454-a574-beabe6f5c8c7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186510522}} {:db/id 17592186051083 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428346 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. two matrices $L$ and $U,$ where

- ![](images/2e/2e6c0b6fdaf90e3a3e23ed91ffe09cb360bb39325b9a630f1b7219b3188a25db.svg) is a *unit lower triangular matrix* (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- ![](images/0c/0c5d7337e47a53dfa5bdce8c6f4a96bb1e52ef6054349011a6cc38f29701cc61.svg) is an *upper triangular matrix*.

For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](images/22/22dba4fe66ac5478f5d81a68342a01809a360de8e722e809998655e7740bafe8.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as 

![](images/d4/d4c92b2e8252619f9a1511d166be884b9a2bdb4311eea8e408e8fe75eed6f36c.svg)

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}}\cdot A \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{L}{{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

**Caution:** In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix $A$ to its *echelon form*:

- we can only add multiples of higher rows to lower rows ($R_j:=R_j+k R_i$ where $i < j$), and

- the other elementary row operations (swapping or multiplying a row by a number) are not allowed." :tutorial/id #uuid "5f8c6994-f448-5679-8d2e-5591b86c2a97" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3178 $$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= (0 - 3)(0 + 2)^{2} \\
&= (-3)(2)^{2} \\
&=-12
\end{aligned}
$$

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-12)$,
- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3$, and
- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-2$.

$$
y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d
$$

where $a >0$, has a characteristic inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape, with $y$-values ranging from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$. This means that every such function has *at least* one real root and *at most* three distinct roots.

For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of

$$
y = x^3-4x^2 +4x
$$

First, we need to find the roots, so we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{3} - 4x^{2} + 4x &= 0 \\
x(x^{2} - 4x + 4) &= 0 \\
x(x - 2)^{2} &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product rule, we get two distinct roots: $x=0$ and $x=2$.

- The root $x=0$ is a *single* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}1}$ because it comes from a factor $x^{\color{blue}1}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}1}$.
- The root $x=2$ is a *double* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}2}$ because it comes from a factor $(x-2)^{\color{blue}2}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}2}$.

To graph the curve, we use the following principles:

- The curve passes through the $x$-axis at the single root (in this case, $x=0$).
- The curve touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root (in this case, $x=2$).

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

"Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{50}∼N(5,{10}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $50$ from a normal population, calculate $P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2).$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.1\,$ | $\,0.5398\,$ | $\,0.5438\,$ | $\,0.5478\,$ | $\,0.5517\,$ | $\,0.5557\,$ |
| $\,0.2\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.5832\,$ | $\,0.5871\,$ | $\,0.5910\,$ | $\,0.5948\,$ |
| $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ | $\,0.6331\,$ |
| $\,0.4\,$ | $\,0.6554\,$ | $\,0.6591\,$ | $\,0.6628\,$ | $\,0.6664\,$ | $\,0.6700\,$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(5,\frac{{10}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(5,2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2) & =P(\frac{4.8-5}{\sqrt{2}}<Z<\frac{5.2-5}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =P(-0.14<Z<0.14) \\  & =Φ(0.14)-Φ(-0.14)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.14)=0.5557,
$$

and by the symmetry of the normal distribution,

$$
\begin{aligned}\,Φ(-0.14) & =1-Φ(0.14) \\  & =1-0.5557 \\  & =0.4443.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(4.8<\overset{―}{X}<5.2) & =Φ(0.14)-Φ(-0.14) \\  & =0.5557-0.4443 \\  & =0.1114.\end{aligned}

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(11,\frac{{12}^{2}}{72}) \\  & ∼N(11,2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(10.75<\overset{―}{X}<11.3).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10.75<\overset{―}{X}<11.3) & =P(\frac{10.75-11}{\sqrt{2}}<Z<\frac{11.3-11}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =P(-0.18<Z<0.21) \\  & =Φ(0.21)-Φ(-0.18)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.21)=0.5832, \\ Φ(-0.18)=0.4286.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(10.75<\overset{―}{X}<11.3) & =Φ(0.21)-Φ(-0.18) \\  & =0.5832-0.4286 \\  & =0.1546.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186444046 :question/id #uuid "1ffa929e-0bc3-5442-add7-2a4161c85ae6" :question/math-academy-id "q-143289" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e13a14a-41e6-597e-a638-642182912501" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5478" :db/id 17592186444016} {:answer/id #uuid "6611d1e3-38dd-5c25-b23c-5999f0cd7010" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5832" :db/id 17592186444026} {:answer/id #uuid "78bfb776-bc5a-5396-9729-eb512c396357" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5120" :db/id 17592186444028} {:answer/id #uuid "7a39b182-f87f-5118-a44d-553dca2a1624" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5517" :db/id 17592186444029} {:answer/id #uuid "94cf0b85-e1f5-5710-9008-25aa3d7d1979" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5040" :db/id 17592186444030}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444028} :answer-field/id #uuid "155d86ce-fd57-5a7a-9d6f-e08f5fc64d99" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444041}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{25}∼N(9,{15}^{2})$ is a random sample of size $25$ from a normal population, calculate $P(\overset{―}{X}<9.08).$

| $\,-0.3\,$ | $\,0.3745\,$ | $\,0.3707\,$ | $\,0.3669\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(2,\frac{{6}^{2}}{18}) \\  & ∼N(2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(|\overset{―}{X}|<1.05).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<1.05) & =P(-1.05<\overset{―}{X}<1.05) \\  & =P(\frac{-1.05-2}{\sqrt{2}}<Z<\frac{1.05-2}{\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =P(-2.16<Z<-0.67) \\  & =Φ(-0.67)-Φ(-2.16)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.67) & =0.2514, \\ Φ(-2.16) & =0.0154.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(|\overset{―}{X}|<1.05) & =Φ(-0.67)-Φ(-2.16) \\  & =0.2514-0.0154 \\  & =0.2360.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162111 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161677 :question/id #uuid "8cbddf16-bfab-539b-bce1-5ccb59dc4313" :question/math-academy-id "e-10087"} :knowledge-point/id | $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| $\,2.7\,$ | $\,0.9965\,$ | $\,0.9966\,$ | $\,0.9967\,$ | $\,0.9968\,$ | $\,0.9969\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$

$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =12,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =0.4,$ and that the sample size $n=100.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(12,\frac{{0.4}^{2}}{100}) \\  & ∼N(12,0.0016).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>12.1).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>12.1) & =P(Z>\frac{12.1-12}{\sqrt{0.0016}}) \\  & =P(Z>2.5) \\  & =1-P(Z<2.5) \\  & =1-Φ(2.5)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(2.5)=0.9938.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>12.1) & =1-Φ(2.5) \\  & =1-0.9938 \\  & =0.0062.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186444045 :question/id #uuid "1449bf6c-a95a-5a03-b860-fb55f8720b4b" :question/math-academy-id "q-143449" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0706cead-5858-5f95-99d1-fa5a1751d466" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3300" :db/id 17592186444015} {:answer/id #uuid "4cde3203-c179-5ba4-ae60-7b4c02c6301c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2981" :db/id 17592186444019} {:answer/id #uuid "4d80c856-f782-53fd-b508-7b19e9123f9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3050" :db/id 17592186444021} {:answer/id #uuid "7176ed6c-39a7-5cdd-9307-0416bd40591e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3015" :db/id 17592186444027} {:answer/id #uuid "f0da8eba-7a84-58c0-a725-444fe641d59d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.3264" :db/id 17592186444035}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444035} :answer-field/id #uuid "f8843340-6adf-5e66-a7c0-bf2cb991f090" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444044}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "The lengths of parchment paper rolls for baking are normally distributed with a mean of $200\,\text{ft}$ and a standard deviation of $10\,\text{ft}.$ Suppose $20$ rolls are randomly selected. {X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =15,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =2,$ and that the sample size $n=16.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(15,\frac{{2}^{2}}{16}) \\  & ∼N(15,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(14.7<\overset{―}{X}<15.3) & =P(\frac{14.7-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{15.3-15}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-0.6<Z<0.6) \\  & =Φ(0.6)-Φ(-0.6)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.6) & ≈0.7257 \\ Φ(-0.6) & ≈0.2743.\end{aligned}
$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

 then the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ has the distribution

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

We're told that the population mean $\mu =20,$ the population standard deviation $\sigma =1,$ and that the sample size $n=50.$ Therefore, the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(20,\frac{{1}^{2}}{50}) \\  & ∼N(20,0.02).\end{aligned}
$$

We're required to find $P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1).$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1) & =P(\frac{19.9-20}{\sqrt{0.02}}<Z<\frac{20.1-20}{\sqrt{0.02}}) \\  & =P(-0.71<Z<0.71) \\  & =Φ(0.71)-Φ(-0.71)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.71) & =0.2389 \\ Φ(0.71) & =0.7611.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(19.9<\overset{―}{X}<20.1) & =Φ(0.71)-Φ(-0.71) \\  & ≈0.7611-0.2389 \\  & =0.5222.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049014} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6578aabd-5f63-5ef9-b370-01df046cf31a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1385" normal population $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2.$ In other words,   

$$
X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n} \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).
$$

In this case, we can easily determine the sampling distribution of the sample mean

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

Recall the following:

- The sum of $n$ independent and identically distributed normal random variables is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
Y = \displaystyle \sum\limits_{i=1}^n X_i
$$

is normally distributed.

- A normally distributed random variable scaled by a constant factor is normally distributed. Thus, 

$$
\overline{X} = \dfrac1n\cdot Y
$$

is normally distributed.

Also, we previously saw that the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean, i.e., 

$$
\textrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu,
$$

and the variance of the sample mean is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\overline{X}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

Putting all of this together, we obtain that

$$
\overline{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),
$$

In other words, the sample mean $\overline{X}$ is normally distributed with mean $\mu$ and variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "14d0c44e-7b46-50e5-800f-e73c03b66e46"
